subtopic: RELIEF AND REHABILITATION IN THE FRASER VALLEY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RELIEF AND REHABILITATION IN THE FRASER VALLEY
speechtext:
I wish to make a statement. on relief and rehabilitation in the Fraser valley as approved by the Premier of British Columbia on behalf of the government of British Columbia and myself on behalf of the government of Canada.
After consultation with the Fraser Valley relief and rehabilitation commission established by the governments of Canada and British Columbia, the two governments have agreed that the assistance to be given by the government of Canada to British Columbia in helping to meet the requirements for emergency relief and for the rehabilitation of the flooded areas in the Fraser valley arising out of the national disaster created by the floods shall take the form of a lump sum grant by the federal to the provincial government of $5,000,000.
It has been agreed by the two governments that this grant will be understood to cover 5849-3701
the share of the government of Canada in temporary emergency relief as well as the share of financial liability for measures of rehabilitation which the government of Canada agreed to accept in accordance with the announcement made in the House of Commons on June 9.
In addition to the lump sum grant of $5,000,000 for relief and rehabilitation, the government of Canada will provide seventy-five per cent of the cost of repairing, strengthening and reconstructing the dikes in the Fraser valley and removing water and debris from the flooded land, and the provincial government will provide the remaining twenty-five per cent of these costs. The two governments have agreed to establish a Fraser Valley diking board that will carry on this work as quickly as the board can be organized and take over the actual responsibility for this work from the various local, provincial and military authorities now dealing with it.
In view of the lump sum grant by the federal to the provincial government, the government of British Columbia, together with the flood relief committee, the Red Cross and the local authorities, will assume responsibility for whatever relief and rehabilitation measures they deem necessary in the flooded areas, not only in the Fraser valley but elsewhere throughout the province, except as regards the repair and reconstruction of the dikes and the removal of water and debris in the Fraser valley. It has also been agreed by the two governments that the armed forces will remain to assist the province until the emergency is ended, and it has been tentatively agreed that the end of the emergency will be regarded as occurring when the water level at Mission falls to eighteen feet.
It was recognized by the provincial government that what the armed forces had already spent on relief would be a part of the $5,000,000 grant, and the amount spent by the armed forces on protecting and repairing the dikes would be a part of the diking costs.
The Canadian army has also undertaken for the present to make available to the diking board a small staff of engineers and the 23rd field squadron of engineers to assist in carrying out a portion of the work. The federal government has designated Mr. F. G. Goodspeed, assistant chief engineer of the Department of Public Works, to share with provincial authorities responsibility for work on the dikes and related matters, and has designated officials of the Department of
Inquiries oj the Ministry

Agriculture and the Department of National Health and Welfare to assist the provincial authorities.
Further supplementary estimates will be introduced in parliament today or tomorrow to provide the authority for the expenditures to be made by the government of Canada under these arrangements; also further supplementary estimates for the special expenditures of the Department of Public Works in its own operations made necessary by the emergency.
While the destruction of property in the Fraser valley reached the proportions of a national disaster, there is reason to be profoundly thankful that so few lives were lost because of the prompt and effective measures taken by members of the armed services as well as by the civil authorities to meet the emergency, and especially because of the magnificent voluntary efforts put forth by the citizens of the province. May I add that the co-operation of the federal and provincial governments in the constructive work of the diking board should give to the people of the Fraser valley a greater sense of security than they have known hitherto for their homes, their families, and their future.
In conclusion, I wish on behalf of the federal government to express warm appreciation of the untiring efforts of the members of the Fraser Valley relief and rehabilitation commission, General Hoffmeister and Hon. Mr. Hamber.

I have your telegram of June 24 and I have copy of the telegram you sent Mr. Matthewson.
There are two phases of the situation which might he mentioned:
The first is that a report which I quote hereunder has reached me and I am sure I do not need to make any comments. These events would have an effect, of course.
Welland

"Sixteen men were moving toward Port Colborne to man the ship John T. Burke tied up at Welland South dock. They were in a panel truck. Near Chambers corners the truck was stopped by a group of men travelling in a lorry, painted red. This group of men attacked the crew, beating them up unmercifully, with the result that five are now in hospital, five are missing and six are suffering from minor injuries.
The Ontario provincial police later impounded a Red-army-style lorry and detained ten men travelling in it."
Montreal-"Last night in Montreal harbour the crew of the S.iS. Mont Sandra went aboard the S.S. Kinmount, which was tied up at No. 3 grain elevator.
They were armed with axes and smashed various parts of the ship's furniture and equipment. They attacked the crew of the Kinmount, injuring four of the men to the extent they had to go to the hospital, and threw the galley stove overboard."

The question who is breaking the law is before the courts; therefore from my point of view the matter is sub judice. Groups of people outside can say all they like about the courts, and they are doing that in some parts of the country. People who ought to know better are doing it. But I cannot express an opinion upon it.
I would say this to my hon. friend-and I think what I say covers the whole field-that it is a difficult situation, as he well knows. I am sorry for both sides to the dispute, although I believe there is a measure of blame on both sides. But there is no use in the labour department, my officials and myself, doing our utmost to settle a dispute of this kind if other parties concerned are going to try to negotiate an agreement through the newspapers. That makes it doubly difficult.
I thought last week, if I may say so at this time, that we had reached a point where the parties concerned would sit down together in the cities of Toronto and Montreal. But circumstances over which I had no control prevented that from happening. I place no blame at the present time. But I do believe this, that you can conduct a strike without this kind of thing about which I have told Mr. Buckley. I do not believe that kind of action helps the Department of Labour, nor does it help the good people on either side of the dispute in the efforts made to bring it to a conclusion.
I hold no brief for the employers in this dispute, but when they are ready to sit down with these people and then get news of that kind-well, I do not know how you can expect any sensible individual to bring the dispute to a successful conclusion.
I do know this, that a good many people who express their views in some of the newspapers of this province think they have the answers to all these questions. They are the people who write the editorial, and who never settled anything in their lives. If they have the answers, I wish they would come forward with them and I will give them good jobs '* my department.

subtopic: CANADA-NEW ZEALAND INCOME TAX AGREEMENT ACT, 1948
speechtext:
The full text of the agreement as signed at Ottawa on the 12th of March, 1948, by the Hon. D. C. Abbott, Minister of Finance for Canada, and the Hon. Walter Nash, Minister of Finance for New Zealand, is set out in the schedule to the bill.
The purpose of the agreement is to avoid, where possible, the double imposition of income and similar taxes where Canadians are carrying on business in New Zealand or otherwise receiving income from New Zealand sources, and where New Zealanders are carrying on business in Canada or otherwise receiving income from Canadian sources, and it also provides that the taxation authorities of the two countries may exchange information which may be necessary to make the agreement effective and to prevent fraud and avoidance of taxes which are subject to the agreement.
The purpose of the bill is to give the agreement the force of law in Canada, and it provides that in the case of inconsistency between the agreement and the operation of any other law, the agreement will prevail to the extent of such inconsistency. The Minister of National Revenue is given the authority to make orders and regulations to carry out the provisions of the agreement, which orders and regulations shall be published in the Canada Gazette and laid before parliament.
The agreement is based on the principles established in the preceding income tax agreements which Canada has made with the United States and the United Kingdom. Double taxation is avoided by a reciprocal system of tax exemptions and tax credits.

speechtext:
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 397, to amend the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act.
He said: This bill proposes a number of changes in the list of items subject to import control under the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act. Before explaining the nature and purpose of these changes, I wish to review briefly the results that have been achieved to date under the program of exchange conservation, and to indicate certain measures of relaxation that may be possible if our reserve position continues to improve at a satisfactory rate over the next few months.
The house will recall that before the introduction of the exchange conservation measures on November 17 of last year, our exchange
5838	COMMONS
Emergency Exchange Conservation Act
reserves, that is to say, our official holdings of gold and United States dollars, were declining at an alarming rate. The figures are familiar enough, and I shall not repeat them on this occasion. It is sufficient for my purpose to recall that during the period from the beginning of 1947 until the middle of November the rate of decline was about 870 million per month, a rate which, if it had continued unchecked, would have exhausted our then remaining reserves of approximately $500 million within a short period-indeed probably before today we would have been completely out of gold and United States dollars.
Drastic action had to be taken, and was taken. The comprehensive program which was developed has been in operation for only about seven months, and indeed, some parts of one aspect of the program, the restriction of capital goods imports, have only recently been put into effect. Nevertheless I am pleased to be able to report that the program is working -working indeed more satisfactorily than I myself had dared to hope. As I shall explain in greater detail in a moment, we have reduced our imports of goods from hard currency areas; we have reduced our travel expenditures in such areas; we have obtained an increasing proportion of our needed supplies from other sources, and we have had a very encouraging increase in our exports to the dollar area as well as to the world as a whole. As a result of these changes in the trend of our trade in goods and services, not only have we stopped the rapid decline in our exchange reserves, but we have reversed the trend and have had an encouraging improvement in our reserve position.
As I have said, our exchange reserves amounted to approximately $500 million when the program was put into effect. They dropped to $461 million on December 17. Knowing the experience of some other countries with somewhat similar programs, we had expected that these reserves would show a further substantial drop before the declining trend could be got under control. That figure for December 17, however, proved to be the low point, and since that time there has been a fairly steady upward trend, wholly apart from the increase in our holdings of United States dollars due to the drawings upon the Export-Import bank loan. On June 23 last, the date of the latest report I have received, they amounted to slightly over $742 million. This total includes $140 million obtained by drawing upon the Export-Import bank loan. If we deduct the amount of these borrowed funds, we have a balance remaining of $602 million,

representing the result of the working of ordinary economic forces.
I think it. will be agreed that the increase thus indicated from the low point of $461 million at December 17 is a gratifying one. It is true, of course, as I indicated in the budget speech, that during the period in question there were one or two items of a special or non-recurring character. These accounted for an increase in our reserves of the order of $60 million. But there were also during the same period offsetting items on the other side, including advances of $112 million to the United Kingdom under the 1946 loan and of about $74 million to other countries under various export credits. As the house knows, drawings on the loan to the United Kingdom have been suspended since mid-April, and the further amount to be drawn by other countries under various export credits will be small; some of these credits have already lapsed, and all will have terminated by the end of the year. I need not remind hon. members that if the portion of our exports so financed could have been sold for cash rather than for credit, there would have been a further increase in our cash reserves of $186 million during the seven months in question. We hope to play a further part in promoting world recovery, within the limits of our reasonable capacity, but we cannot continue to do so on the scale of the recent past, and thanks to the assistance which western Europe will now secure from the European recovery program approved by the United States Congress, that should no longer be necessary.
While I have expressed a large measure of satisfaction, and indeed of gratification, with the results up to date of the exchange conservation program, I wish to emphasize that we cannot as yet afford to be complacent. We have still a considerable distance to go before we can regard our holdings of gold and United States dollars as satisfactory. We must continue to increase those holdings to the point where they will be adequate to meet the drains which will undoubtedly occur from time to time-whether due to internal boom and consequent high imports, or to internal misfortune such as a crop failure and consequent low exports, or to the financial difficulties of some of our best customers, or to worldwide economic fluctuations. But while we must face realistically the task still ahead of us, we have reason to be proud of the progress already made.
Each part of the exchange conservation program has contributed to the improvement in our exchange reserves which I have described. I am informed that the limitation

___________Emergency Exchange Conservation Act
on travel funds has effected very substantial savings of United States dollars, and I wish to pay tribute to the way in which Canadians have accepted this very necessary but nevertheless vexatious restriction on their freedom of movement across the border. I am also gratified by the friendly attitude of our American neighbours who might well have misunderstood our motives, but who are, in fact, visiting this country in great numbers-considerably larger numbers, I believe, than last year.
A few days ago figures were released to the public, showing the effects upon imports of the restrictions imposed upon items included in schedules I and II of the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act during the first quarter of 1948. Note: The above tables compare imports of goods covered by Schedules I and II of the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act during the first four months of 1948 with the corresponding statistics for 1947. It will be noted that some imports continue to be shown under the prohibited list of Schedule I during the first four months of 1948. This arises out of the fact that not all of the commodities included in the statistical classification under which imports are classified were covered by the prohibitions. Also in certain instances permits were granted to deal with cases of exceptional hardship, as provided in the Act.
The figures in these tables show that imports from scheduled countries, that is, the United States and certain other dollar countries, under schedules I and II were $86 million less during the first four months of 1948 than during the corresponding period of 1947. Goods which were prohibited under schedule I accounted for $31,000,000 of the decrease, and those placed under quota by schedule II for the remaining $55,000,000. The average monthly decrease in imports from these scheduled countries was thus $20-5 million in the first four months of this year as compared with the first four months of last year.
Turning to imports from non-scheduled countries, that is, countries which might roughly be termed non-dollar countries or countries which are also short of dollar exchange, the results are equally satisfactory, though for a. different reason. As hon. members know, the government adopted a policy of non-discrimination in its import restrictions as being the best policy from Canada's long-term point of view as a trading nation. In applying that policy an attempt was made, however, to place as few restrictions as possible on trade with non-scheduled countries. The results for the first four months show that imports from soft currency countries of goods listed in schedules I and II of the aot were 32 per cent higher in the first four months of

1948 than in the first four months of 1947. British trade has been affected scarcely at all by the prohibitions under schedule I, and it has already begun to benefit considerably from the operation of quotas under schedule II.
My colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) gave to the house a detailed survey of the results of operations under schedule III of the act, which comes under his jurisdiction, and there is therefore no need for me to repeat (the information he gave. However, I do think it worthy of comment that during the past seven months it has been possible for us to continue to import the capital goods and materials required to enable us to carry on the expansion of our industrial capacity which has been under way since the conclusion of hostilities. As my colleague emphasized, the program is designed not merely to save dollars in the short run, but also to help us to solve our long-run problem of achieving a better balance in our trading relationship with the dollar area.
As the government has endeavoured to make clear on a number of occasions, our approach to the dollar problem is essentially a positive approach. We introduced restrictions with the greatest reluctance, and only because they were vitally necessary to stem the decline in our reserves. In any event, as I have already outlined, they have had the desired results. But

Emergency Exchange Conservation Act
the government is much more gratified by the increase that has taken place in our earnings from exports. In each month since the turn of the year the value of our commodity exports to the United States has exceeded that for the corresponding month of 1947 by a substantial amount, the increase for the whole period from January 1 to May 31 being $136 million, or approximately 34 per cent. Making the same comparison for exports to all countries, the increase is $111 million, or 10J per cent.
The future is a matter of uncertainty, and I would be the last to indulge in gratuitous prophecy. But I do think that the results achieved dwing the past seven months, on both the negative and positive sides of the program, are such that I should indicate at this time that, if serious setbacks do not occur in the meantime, the government plans to relax the restrictions on the imports of certain goods that are habitually consumed by Canadians and are looked upon as highly desirable, if not altogether essential.
In particular, the government believes that it will be possible towards the end of 1948 to take certain of the commonly consumed fresh fruits and vegetables off the prohibited list and put them under quota so as to permit Canadian consumers to obtain a reasonable quantity of this fresh produce when domestic supplies are beginning to become relatively scarce.
This indication of policy is in line with the statement which I gave in reply to a question of the hon. member for Fraser Valley, which appears on page 1431 of Hansard for February 20, 1948. At that time I said:
As I now see the situation and as I now view the prospects of our exchange position I think it is highly improbable that a complete removal of these restrictions with respect to fresh fruits and vegetables will occur much before the end of this calendar year, and it may be that some degree of restriction will continue into the early part of 1949. As far as possible it would be the government's intention not to remove or relax these import controls at a time when that action would have serious or disastrous effects on the marketing of Canadian produce. But I cannot bind the government to any unconditional guarantee that no produce grown in Canada in 1948 will have to face any competition from imported goods. As I said nearly three months ago, the government intends to relax restrictions on basic or essential items such as cabbages, carrots, potatoes, and onions when it becomes clear that Canadian supplies are nearing exhaustion.
As hon. members know, the government (has already permitted limited importation from time to time of certain fresh vegetables, such as cabbages, carrots, potatoes and onions.
Furthermore, the government is hopeful that importations of citrus fruits which are
now under quota will continue to be available in at least as large quantities as up to now and if possible that the quotas will be enlarged.
Meanwhile, steps will be taken to authorize the resumption next winter of imports cVf British West Indies tomatoes, which for a number of years, since the application of a high tariff against them by the United States, have been grown especially for the Canadian market. These imports will be subject to quota limitations related to imports from that area in recent years.
Summing up the situation in so far as fresh fruits and vegetables are concerned,
I expect that next winter, while we may have to continue restricting the importation of the less commonly used and more expensive items, it will be possible to have available not only adequate supplies of citrus fruits but also reasonable supplies of such staple vegetables of widespread consumption as lettuce, celery and tomatoes at a time when Canadian supplies are not available.
I now turn to the contents of the bill that is before the house. The amendments to schedules I and II are few in number and simple in character. The amendments to schedule III are more extensive, but they are in large part merely consequential upon changes in tariff wordings which were made in the budget in order to provide for reduced rates of duty on various imported materials and components required by Canadian industries. They will be dealt with by my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I wish to summarize briefly the proposed changes in schedules I and II, for which I am responsible. These changes will be brought provisionally into force as of tomorrow. The Minister of Trade and Commerce will deal with schedule HI later.
Schedule I. Three of the seven changes which it is proposed to make in schedule I are merely clarifications; two broaden existing provisions to cover goods which may be imported in substitution for other goods which are already prohibited, and two involve the addition of completely new items. The combined effect of these changes is expected to be a substantial additional saving of foreign exchange and more equitable treatment as between competitive or partially competitive products. The substance of the various amendments is as follows:
(a)	The explanatory note at the head of schedule I is expanded in order to make it clear that no description in the prohibited

Emergency Exchange Conservation Act
list shall be deemed to include any goods classified under a tariff item listed in schedule H.
(b)	A new item is inserted to cover acoustical wallboards, pads and tile of any material. Acoustical wallboard of wood fibre was already covered, but similar or competitive products made of asbestos or gypsum were not.
(c)	The gummed paper item is reworded to make it clear that it applies to printed as well as to unprinted gummed paper.
(d)	A new item is inserted to cover synthetic resin soft sheets or strips, and manufactures thereof. It includes such products as plastic shower curtains, aprons, tablecloths, et cetera, and the pliable sheeting from which they are made. It does not include the hard plastic materials which are used extensively for structural and industrial purposes. Nor does it apply to any articles included in schedule II. They will remain subject to quota without change.
(e)	The item covering mirrors is expanded to include mirrors of glass coated with any material. Formerly it applied only to silvered glass.
(f)	A new item is inserted to cover asphalt tile.
(g)	A provision which is no longer necessary, by reason of the addition of the proviso to the note at the beginning of the schedule, is repealed.
Schedule II. Three items are inserted in category 4 of schedule II. They cover vacuum cleaners, motorcycles, bicycles and tricycles.
Bicycles and tricycles are a new addition to the schedule which appears desirable in view of a sharp increase in imports from scheduled countries. Vacuum cleaners and motorcycles are being transferred from schedule III to schedule II, and imports from scheduled countries will be subject to quota. Production parts will remain subject to control under schedule IN.
While the effect of the bill is to impose some further restrictions on imports, the new items do not differ in character from the items already included in the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act. They are designed to effect savings in dollar exchange where least harm will be done to the economy as a whole and to leave greater resources available for the importation of the more essential items.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few brief comments to make on what the minister has said. I should perhaps have been more impressed by the minister's statement if it had been shorter. I was rather reminded of the remark, "Methinks the lady doth protest too much". The minister was at pains to point out that everything was lovely, but I was not sure, as he read the statement, that everything was in fact quite as satisfactory as he suggested. However, some progress has been made, and we should be unaffectedly glad. I confess further that when the minister says that everything is good, or pretty good, and in the next breath tells us that he has had to draw down $140 million of the $300 million, I have a sense of disturbance and the feeling that all is not so well.
We must remember that by the unwise policy pursued until November of last year the government precipitated a perfect spate of buying so that there was bound to be something of a reaction. We need not therefore take too much comfort from the improved figures; nevertheless, to the extent that there is an improvement, we should take what comfort we can.
I would remind the house that notwithstanding the very favourable picture the minister has attempted to give us, we have had to draw in our horns a bit with regard to the credits we were hoping to make, and to take the view that our position does not warrant our doing just what we had hoped to do, and that to me is also regrettable.
The minister explained how the various measures had worked effectively, but I do not find any attempt made to give any figure to show the effectiveness of the blessed 25 per cent austerity tax. It may be that the suggestion of the report that has been freely circulated, though I understand without warrant, may be realized a little later than

the month of December, as the minister now tells us. I understand there are gentlemen sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker, who would like to question the December date and bring it as close to us as June.

speechtext:
Perhaps I might supplement the remarks of my hon. friend by a description of the bill as it applies to amendments to part III of the act.
Category III provides for some further amendments in wording in order to conform with the revised Customs Act and for bringing radio repair parts under control. Category IV similarly brings under control all radio repair parts not covered in III, and also all parts of electric light fixtures and electric appliances. In the past, repair parts, with the exception of automobile repair parts, have been admitted freely and without requiring a permit. It has been found very difficult, however, except in a few cases, to distinguish between imports of repair parts and imports of similar parts for production purposes. In these circumstances it appears fairer all round to put imports of all parts under control and on a quota basis.
Category V covers amendments which, I believe, will provide for better administration. In the four tariff item numbers affected, it is proposed to delete that part of the wording which provides that permits will not be necessary for importations which do not exceed a certain value. Experience has shown that a more specific definition is required to cover such exclusions, and it is proposed, subject to this amendment being approved, that a type of general permit will be provided under each of the tariff items noted, to allow for what might be termed "casual importations," to values not exceeding the values now stated in the act, which are made by an importer for his own use and which are not intended for resale.
It will be noted that minor changes are proposed to the wording and punctuation of certain of the items. These changes become necessary to define the meaning of the items included in the act and are in accordance with the accepted wording of the customs tariff.
Category VI brings fibre glass and glass wool and a number of industrial chemicals into schedule III. Fibre glass imports were originally prohibited, but the prohibition was removed by order in council when it was established that imports were essential for insulation in various appliances such as refrigerators and stoves. Imports have increased substantially from $938,000 in 1947 to current annual rate of $1,400,000. It now appears that the imported fibre glass is being used for a number of general insulation purposes which could be quite satisfactorily served by Canadian products. By including fibre glass in schedule III it will be possible to restrict imports to those essential for technical reasons for certain specialized insulation requirements.
Imports of the industrial chemicals which it is now proposed to include in schedule III totalled something over seven and a half million dollars in 1947. It is believed that it is now possible, as a result of improvements in the domestic supply position, to save some appreciable amount of exchange on these items.
Perhaps this is an opportune time to make a few observations on the general development and progress of our capital goods import control-.the administration of schedule III. On June 10 last I gave a detailed review of the statistical results of our controls to date, and a description of our organizational approach and procedure. I need not reiterate the details of what I said before, but I should review briefly the record of .the administration of schedule III up to the present.
To begin with, it must be appreciated that the problems in administering schedule III are very different from those of schedules I and n. The administration of all the schedules is directed to the same objective, of course-to conserving United States dollars; but from the very nature of the different commodities and situations with which they deal, the methods adopted must be different. Schedules I and II are designed primarily to cut down imports of consumer goods which we can, in a pinch, do without. Schedule III is designed primarily to control and direct imports of capital goods to the most constructive .purposes and best national advantage from an exchange point of view.
The dollar value of imports from the United States of goods enumerated in schedule HI was held at $187 million in the first four months of

1948. This represents a reduction, although not a large reduction, from the levels reached by these same imports in 1947. The larger part of the savings so far is accounted for by automotive vehicles and parts, where my original estimate of a S75 million saving in 1948 is well on the way to being realized. Other items have been brought under control from time to time, many of them at very recent dates; so that the full effect of the program is not yet apparent in .the import statistics. With a new list of items announced to take effect on June 26, eighty-nine per cent of the original schedule III items have been brought under control, and these accounted for ninety-six per cent of all the imports in schedule HI in 1947.
Three different methods have been followed in the detailed administration of the schedule III items. These procedures have been developed as being appropriate in each case to meet the needs of the problems which were encountered. Dollar allotments are issued to manufacturers who are importers of parts for production use enumerated in schedule III. These vary a good deal from one industry to another, but they follow the general lines of the formula established in the automobile industry, which latter has been published in detail. Up to the present, about 1,200 of these dollar allotments have been issued.
In cases not subject to dollar allotments, import permits are issued on an individual basis to cover the particular shipment concerned. Up to the end of May, $21-5 million of import authorizations were granted in this way. The third meithod of control is project approvals, which cover all imports necessary for a particular construction project or industrial plant. These project approvals are, in effect, an assurance to the builder concerned that individual shipment permits will be issued as they are needed.
The whole program has been developing in a very substantial and encouraging way. I gave some concrete examples in my statement on June 10. Substantial expansion is planned, and is now getting under way, in a number of important manufacturing fields affected by the import restrictions. From automobiles to automobile parts, radar to television, typewriters to washing machines, micro-motors to buses, heating pads to penicillin, Venetian blinds to asbestos cement pipe, biscuits to grape juice, we have new products and new industries springing up weekly. A pattern has developed which we think is a seund economic approach to the problem of the best distribution of activity between United States parent companies and Canadian branch plants. A number of arrangements have been worked out by which the Canadian plant concentrates 
on a standard model for both the domestic market and for export, and the United States parent turns over the export markets for this particular model to the Canadian plant. This is, of course, a feasible proposition only if the Canadian plant can meet the United States plant costs. I am glad to say that in most of the cases we have examined it was clear that the Canadian plant, on the mass production basis which the export orders made possible, could compete advantageously with the United States plant.
There are long-run implications of this development of particular interest to us. There may have been, some element of pressure in inaugurating these developments, but they have proceeded only because the companies concerned are satisfied that they are basically sound and economically advantageous. While the exchange and import restrictions are, we hope, of temporary duration, the stimulus given Canadian industry, the new markets found for Canadian products, the recognition of Canadian industrial and cost advantages, are all constructive factors which will continue.
Our natural resources development programs also have long-range objectives in view. It is not enough for us to consolidate our wartime industrial expansion, or to meet our exchange problem solely by defensive means. We must build for the future, and build on the basis of an economically sound international division of labour. It is by this method, and this method only, that we shall assure a balanced position for our foreign trade, which is of such great importance to our general economy. Consequently, I welcome the evidence that new investment in Canada is looked upon as not only sound from the point of view of supplying the domestic market, but as advantageous in supplying all world markets open to us.
An interesting development in this connection has been in the motion picture business. A group which includes all the major United States motion picture units has formed an association known as the Canadian Co-operation Project. The specific objective of this project is to make what contribution the movie industry can to a solution of our exchange problem, and more specifically to spread general information about Canada and whip up tourist interest. As an example of the efforts of this group, while there were 61 Canadian subjects in American newsreels in 1947, there have already been 64 this year. Just yesterday contracts were concluded covering some $2,000,000 to $3,000,000 of feature productions in Canada, which Canadian interests are financing on approximately a fifty-fifty basis, and from which Canada will

________Emergency Exchange Conservation Act
get a pro rata share of vorld earnings. A number of other commitments, chiefly for short features of tourist interest, have been made and others are being negotiated. In view of the way the American movie industiy is plugging Canada, the least I can do is plug the production "Neighbour to the North" which is appearing at a local theatre. This will give an idea of the type of assistance, which cannot always be measured in dollars but which has very important dollar importance, whieh this industry can give.
We are accused on one side of a new protectionism, and on the other of a new socialist dictatorship. We are accused at one and the same time of not doing enough in a positive way to encourage Canadian industry and economic expansion, and of encouraging so much that we are intensifying an already highly inflationary situation. As usual, the truth lies somewhere between the two extremes.
There has been, of course, an inevitable but temporary element of protectionism in banning imports of a number of consumer goods in high demand in Canada, but at the same time steps have been taken to expand competitive production in Canada and to stimulate exports, even at the expense of some continuing shortages in the domestic market. On the other hand, these measures have not been forcibly imposed on defenceless industry by a dictatorial bureaucracy: they have been worked out with the wholehearted co-operation of responsible industry in this country by the simple expedient of putting the facts of the situation in each case squarely before the industry concerned. This means that there is nothing immediately spectacular in our positive program-no highly advertised five year government plans-but we do know that we are building firmly and practically.
If anything, we have more cause for concern over the criticism that we are attempting too much than that we are not doing enough. The magnitude of the current investment boom in Canada is almost alarming. We forecast new capital investment, in 1948, of S2-8 billion at the beginning of the year; the indications are that this will be exceeded. Fortunately we have been able to arrange for increased supplies of basic products and building materials required in this connection, and the more essential parts of the program, such as housing, and necessary industrial and utility expansion, have not been delayed. In fact, we are already reaching a stage at which the very large capital investments made both during and after the war are beginning to pay off materially in increased production. I would not minimize, however, the pressure that continues on scarce supplies-on construction
labour of all kinds, on key materials such as steel, and of course, on our United States dollars and the things that must be imported from the United States.
There is a fundamental point I would like to emphasize. Our exchange problem and the measures we have taken to meet it arise directly from the terrible destruction of the last war. I refer not only to the human and material destruction, but to the breakdown of the former international exchange and trade systems and to the loss of free government institutions in some parts of the world. At the same time we have on this continent, and in this country, employment, production, income, and, in general, prosperity and standards of living higher than ever before.
I am sure that most Canadians do not appreciate the tremendous strides Canada has made in the world scene in the last decade. We are today the third trading nation in the world, by quite a wide margin. Our wartime industrial development was no flash in the pan; we have gone on since the war, converted and expanded, and our industrial efficiency and output today compare favourably with that of any other country in the world. I could reel off a list of first in every field, from housing construction and family allowances to power developments and paper production, that bear witness to our productivity and, I should add, to our good fortune.
We who are sitting here have been privileged to see Canada grow from economic adolescence to maturity, and to become one of the leading commercial and industrial countries of the world. It almost seems that we have profited from the war destruction and the necessary post-war rehabilitation. But I think on this our conscience can be clear. We have done more per capita to assist European recovery than has any other country. We intend to continue contributing to the extent of our resources, in co-operation with the United States, through the Marshall European recovery program. Apart from any other considerations it is obviously in our long-run interests to do what we can to restore the basis for a free world trading economy. This will require some degree of sacrifice from this country, some temporary abstinence, some restrictions on otherwise worthwhile projects. To make an effective contribution to European recovery we must develop a substantial over-all surplus of exports. To some extent we can do this by producing more. To some extent we shall have to do it oy consuming less. Every export from Canada has an appreciable United States dollar-content, direct or indirect. Until there is a greater degree of multilateral trade, and

until exchange convertibility can be restored, we must maintain controls that will reduce our less essential imports from the United States, and also controls that will direct imports in the capital goods field to their most useful purpose. The latter controls are the particular responsibility of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the best effort of that department is being directed toward administering these controls fairly and efficiently, in the best interests of Canada's financial stability.

Mr. Speaker, the statements of the two ministers are indeed important and extremely interesting. Taking them together, as the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) has said, we should not refrain from giving what credit may be due and expressing satisfaction with what progress is being made. With the hon. member, however, I do feel that if the government or the ministers wish to take credit for the way in which this program is working, we should be careful to see that they are really justified in doing so.
The figures given by both ministers, first as to the increase in our reserve of American dollars, and second as to the change in the export trade picture, are quite impressive. As has been pointed out, however, the increase in our United States dollar reserve is not so impressive when it is remembered that $140 million is the result of our drawing upon a loan.
The other comment I wish to make in that connection is that while we may be building up slightly larger supplies of United States dollars, we have not yet reached the stage where we can say with confidence that our trade situation is such as to enable us even to start looking toward the removal of these controls. If we do, our supply of United States dollars will immediately rush down the drain again. We have no more United States dollars than we had when this program was started last November, and I do not think we have seen anything which would lead us to assume that we have yet gone very far in changing the trade picture along the road to the eventual goal of being able to take off these controls. In fact, even although the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) says the government has this point in mind, the industries we are building up, and the pattern of development we are undertaking, is inevitably being built up within what must be the narrow limits of controls, and of the policy which the minister has in his mind.
Instead of enabling us to take off those controls, the effect may be the very opposite,

namely, to compel us to keep them on. In other words, the more we build up these things with controlled exchange, and the more we operate along those lines while not permitting it to operate along other lines, the more urgent it becomes to keep those particular lines going and, as a result, to keep the same controls. Certainly in these circumstances more pressure will be put on by the industries which have been built up under that system. They will press not to change the situation and not to expose them to the vagaries of free exchange and free competition from without our borders.
That was the danger we saw when this program was inaugurated. We are pleased that we have actually got more United States dollars than we had at that time; but we do not think that the danger has been lessened in any way. We think our Canadian economy is built up along what are in fact unsound lines, lines which will eventually compel us to keep those very controls which on all sides, when the program was begun, were admitted to be undesirable.
If we have come to the point where we can relax restrictions and contemplate imports which will cost us United States dollars, if the situation has been eased to that extent, then it seems to me that instead of doing this -or certainly as well as doing this-we can take at least more items out from under the 25 per cent excise tax, which forms the other side of the program. I believe as a matter of fact that it would be better to give that relief before giving this relaxation, or the type of relief along the lines indicated in the bill.
Where it is applied, obviously the 25 per cent tax increases the cost of living. I shall not embark upon a long dissertation upon the cost of living. I have no doubt the minister has received as many representations in the matter as he cares to receive. Biut he cannot deny that this cost of living increase, apart altogether 'from the economic side of the picture, is having a serious effect upon the outlook of the people of Canada. They are beginning to wonder whether governments care very much what happens to the cost of living.
It is important economically, certainly, and it is also important from the .point of view that the people are finding it difficult to meet that rising cost. Everything that can be done should be done as soon as possible to reduce the cost. Instead of giving relief by releasing import restrictions, or certainly as well as doing that, there should be further relaxation of the 25 per cent excise tax by taking some of the items out from under that tax.

Mr. Speaker, wihat I have t-o say will be brief. It seems to me, however, that statements as important as those made this morning by the two ministers ought not to pass without one further comment. What I have to say has to do with what Canada is being paid for these exports about which the minister spoke when he said that United States subsidiaries here are taking over the export market for their parent companies.
If we are being paid in United States dollars, that is fine. If we are being paid in sterling credits, thus adding to Canada's sterling credit situation, that is not so good. But if we are being paid in Canadian dollars which our government has lent these other countries then we are in the position of financing exports of the subsidiaries of companies in a foreign country. Will the minister tell us exactly the currency in which we are being . paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Convertible currency for everything, except what is sent under United Kingdom credits or credits to the other western European nations. We do not deal on any other basis. It is cash.
A cash basis, fully convertible?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; we cannot afford to do anything else.

I do not propose to take much time of the committee, but I do wish to comment on one phrase used by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, one to which I listened with considerable interest. I refer to his statement to the effect that investments are developing at an almost alarming rate, and that the investments are chiefly investments in capital goods.
Let me say to the minister, when he speaks of alarm, that the present situation is due largely to the measures he took himself by reason of the extravagant double depreciation.
I would remind him further of what I said in the house before, that the present cost of living is due in some measure, even in substantial measure, to the fact that goods and services and labour have been taken away from commodities which sustain the life of the consumer, and put into capital goods. When the minister says he is alarmed I would remind him that the alarm is justified, and is brought about by a condition which in substantial measure he has created.

I can see nothing in the bill to determine the method employed to regulate the value of the Canadian dollar. This is a bill to amend the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act. What rule of procedure did the government employ to determine the artificial value of the Canadian dollar? In the ordinary course of events the dollar would have been at a discount of ten per cent, and had it been allowed to seek its own level it probably would have receded still further. Be that as it may-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Would it be proper to ask what regulation is passed to determine the value of the Canadian dollar?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

When the minister says "fully convertible", what does he mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I mean in hard currency, in cash, in currency which can be converted into United States dollars, which is the currency we want. If we sell in the Argentine the exporter must get his payment either in United States dollars or in a currency such as Swiss francs, which is convertible into United States dollars. In other words, we cannot afford to sell except, for hard currency, or currency which we can convert into United States dollars. It will have to be either gold or convertible exchange.

This might be a good place for the minister to express his well-known sympathy toward those who require kerosene operated refrigerators. Could a small quota not be provided which would show what our intentions are? I do not think the minister fully appreciates how the people in a riding such as mine get along. We do not have many of the summer campers and luxury tourists for whom the minister is afraid to provide these kerosene operated refrigerators and thus create a loss in foreign exchange. Many people in my riding are able to get fresh vegetables not more than once a week. The hon. member for Vancouver North says that the same thing applies to his riding. No ice is available, and these people cannot go down to a corner store to buy fresh vegetables or fresh meat because the store is not usually a large enough establishment to have an alternative method of refrigeration. I think if the minister would give some thought to this he could even offer an amendment now. I would be most grateful to have it as a gesture of good intentions toward these folk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I indicated a moment ago in my statement, in rather guarded terms it is true, that I contemplated that if we continued to improve our position, we would be making a progressive relaxation. I felt that this fall we might be able to establish reasonable quotas for fresh fruits and vegetables such as lettuce, tomatoes and celery. I will say to my hon. friend that having regard to the general indication of relaxation which I gave, I think it will be possible to give early consideration to the establishment of a quota for kerosene operated refrigerators.
I concur in the remarks of the hon. member because what he has said would apply to many people in small towns in British Columbia.

I would point out that summer is here, and those who live in out-of-the-way places find it difficult to get along without these refrigerators. The other day I referred to the minister a case in which a man was able to get in supplies only once a week, and he needed to have some way of keeping those supplies. I am glad the minister intends to give consideration to this matter, but I hope he will be able to do something before the hot weather is at its 'height.

The Minister of Finance said that these changes in the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act will affect substantial savings of exchange. Does he mean we shall have to go still further with the imposition of restrictive measures, which he appears to dislike and which the people of Canada abhor?
Taking the exchange reserves as of December 17, 1947, the low point, as being S461 million; then taking the present position and adjusting for pluses and minuses, I note that we are up $189 million. Eighty-six million dollars of that came through savings effected under schedules I and II. If I remember correctly, there was no great saving under schedule III, under the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because of the great expansion in manufacturing facilities. If I am wrong, he will correct me.
What I should like to find out from the combined ministers is whether of the $189,000,000 which we have added to our exchange reserves, $86,000,000 approximately has come from these restrictions and $103,000,000 from the normal trade channels ex no legislative restrictions whatsoever. I feel that if we have bettered our position through these restrictions only to that extent, then we are simply applying a palliative; we are not getting to the root of our troubles, and the outlook is bleak.
I would feel much better about the whole matter if I thought that our ordinary commerce position was such that we were rectifying our exchange position by natural means, and perhaps through some of the constructive means which the Minister of Trade and Commerce said would be undertaken and which are now perhaps in operation to some extent. Will the minister let me know whether my calculation is approximately correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to think that the saving was $189,000,000, but unfortunately it is $141,000,00. The difference in our reserve position as between the low point of December 17, 1947, and June 23, 1948, excluding our Export-Import bank borrowings, is $141,000,000, the difference between $602,000,000 as of the latter and $461,000,000, which was the low

Emergency Exchange Conservation Act
point on December 17. That represents our exchange receipts from all sources, including invisibles such as the tourist trade. It is impossible to pin-point any portion of it and say that that was due to the restrictive side of the program, but the figures which I mentioned in my speech indicate an estimated saving on last year's figures as a result of the restrictive programs. What our imports would have been without the restrictive program, no one can say.
On balance the position is this: Our net reserve position has shown a moderate but steady improvement, and that has been due both to the restrictive measures which were imposed and to the positive measures in the form of increased exports to dollar areas, which have been substantial.

I should like to be right on these figures. I understand that on June 23 we had 8742,000,000 in reserve. I have deducted from that the $140,000,000 which came from the Export-Import bank. That leaves $602,000,000. Then the minister mentioned that there were certain non-recurring items of $60,000,000 which we should deduct. I do not know what they were, but that makes $542,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

What part has the loan played in these plans?

Even when we include the $140 million we have already drawn upon the Export-Import bank loan, the figure is still too low. The minister led me up the wrong alley. I put the figures down as he was speaking. I draw the minister's
attention to the underlined words in section 1(a):
Provided that where any goods described in this schedule are included in a tariff item listed in schedule II, those goods shall not be deemed to be included in this schedule but shall be deemed to be included in schedule II.

subtopic: TRANSACTIONS BV CANADIAN RESIDENTS, IN CANADA AND ELSEWHERE

speechtext:
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 396. to amend the Foreign Exchange Control Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1

Buy apd sell foreign currency only from and to authorized dealers.

subtopic: TRANSACTIONS BV CANADIAN RESIDENTS, IN CANADA AND ELSEWHERE
speechtext: Is the minister going to say anything about this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TRANSACTIONS BV CANADIAN RESIDENTS, IN CANADA AND ELSEWHERE
speechtext:
I do not know that there is much I can add to what I said yesterday when the bill was introduced. Its purpose is to close a loophole which it had not been realized existed in the act. The loophole was brought to the attention of the officers of the control board as the result of a case in the magistrate's court in Toronto. The facts of the case were these: A Canadian resident in Toronto, between September 1946 and April 1947, bought in the United States about $15,000 worth of cameras which were shipped to him in Niagara Falls, New York, c.o.d. Evidence was given at the trial by two witnesses from Buffalo and Niagara Falls, New York, who produced and identified the original records of the railway express agency under which this man was shown to have received the shipments at Niagara Falls, New York, and that he paid therefor at the railway express agency office amounts totalling about $15,248 in United States currency. Four other witnesses gave evidence indicating that this man was ordinarily resident in Canada.
At the conclusion of the evidence for the prosecution, counsel for the defence argued that there was nothing to show that the accused had received in Canada any part of the moneys paid for the shipments, and that sections 19 and 22 do not impose obligations on residents with respect to transactions taking place entirely outside Canada. The magistrate accepted this argument and dismissed the charges. An appeal has been taken.
As I said yesterday, the intention of course in drafting the Foreign Exchange Control Act was that so far as it relates to transactions by residents it should have extraterritorial effect; and in most sections this is made clear by the use of the words "in Canada or elsewhere". The committee will appreciate that if it is maintained, this decision would seriously prejudice the administration of the act, since it would mean that any Canadian resident who obtained payment of United States funds while in the United States-for example, for exports from Canada-could dispose of the funds there without committing an offence.
I believe the committee will realize that in order to carry out the intent and purpose of the Foreign Exchange Control Act, if this decision in Toronto is sound, the loophole must be plugged. In other sections the expression "in Canada or elsewhere" is used, but in these sections, numbers 19 to 22, for some reason those words are not used.

subtopic: TRANSACTIONS BV CANADIAN RESIDENTS, IN CANADA AND ELSEWHERE
speechtext:
I am sure that we all agree that however bad or regrettable a law may be, when it is on the statute book we must not allow it to be made a fool of. So far as this measure is necessary I have no comment to make with respect to it. But I do draw to the attention of the minister the fact that section 22, as it will now read, will be very broad indeed. It states:
Every resident, other than an authorized dealer who, either in Canada or elsewhere, has or acquires the ownership or possession of foreign currency-
Foreign Exchange Control Act

And so on. That applies to a person going to the United States, who, not through any commercial transaction at all, but by reason of his relationship or friendship with some other persons, may receive some money. He would then come under the purview of this section. In effect he would thereby become liable. Is that a fact, and if so, could not the minister devise some amendment which would not apply to that kind of case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TRANSACTIONS BV CANADIAN RESIDENTS, IN CANADA AND ELSEWHERE
speechtext: There would be no intention of attacking a case' such as the hon. member has described. The general rule envisaged under the act is that a resident of Canada who comes into the possession of dollar exchange is obliged to account for it, as the act says, to the authorized dealer, who in effect is the Minister of Finance. The case my hon. friend has in mind is that of a man who might be down in the United States and who would have obtained a permit to go there. A friend might give him S50, which he would be free to use. I suppose the hon. member is suggesting he might be committing a breach of the law if he did not turn it in.

subtopic: TRANSACTIONS BV CANADIAN RESIDENTS, IN CANADA AND ELSEWHERE
speechtext: I am not suggesting many people w-ould have consciences as delicate as that of the minister. But would it not be possible to make it clear just what is meant? I imagine the intention is to apply to moneys which would develop in the course of business transactions, and not in the course of ordinary personal relationships. Is that a fair statement of the situation? If it is, then it seems to me the bill as it stands now goes too far.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TRANSACTIONS BV CANADIAN RESIDENTS, IN CANADA AND ELSEWHERE
speechtext: There is no change in the law as it stands, except to make it applicable to Canadian residents outside their own country. I think the intent of the act is that those of us who come into possession of foreign exchange-and I refer more particularly to United States dollars-are obligated to turn that money in. We are obligated to turn in to the common pool any surplus which we are not entitled to use legitimately. I do not know how we can change this particular section to give any greater safeguard to individual Canadians who might be travelling in the United States. I can assure the committee that we have no desire to persecute people, but without this change there would be a glaring loophole in the law which would be completely improper if allowed to remain there, and to remain unchanged.

subtopic: TRANSACTIONS BV CANADIAN RESIDENTS, IN CANADA AND ELSEWHERE
speechtext:
Let us suppose a Canadian has received an inheritance in the United States. He is entitled to a payment out of the estate of, we will say, his uncle. He wants to

leave it down there and lend it to somebody else. 'Could he do that, or would he be precluded from doing so by section 22?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TRANSACTIONS BV CANADIAN RESIDENTS, IN CANADA AND ELSEWHERE
speechtext: I 'have not my officials 'before me. I think the policy up to the present time has been to allow Canadian residents to retain investments in the United States, subject of course to the obligation of turning in to the exchange control board the revenues received from those investments. Mind you, the act must be broad enough to enable the exchange control board, if it becomes necessary to do so, to take over all foreign investments. The act has always had that provision in it, as other exchange control acts have. Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a moment or two to answer the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
Last evening, in discussing mobility of labour, the hon. member for Cape Breton South was of the opinion that the arrangements which unemployed men in certain areas of the maritimes could be furnished with transportation to other places in Canada where jobs were available had been cancelled. He said he understood I had made a statement to that effect in this house. I think he is mistaken, and if I gave any such impression,
I was mistaken. The fact is that the arrangements in regard to providing transportation to move men to employment have not been cancelled, and have been in effect since early in 1947.
On February 17, page 1283 of Hansard, I made a statement of this kind reporting on the progress of the transfers, and my parliamentary assistant made a further and more extended statement on June 16 last, that latter statement appearing on page 5284 of Hansard.
In his statement my parliamentary assistant discussed a movement of men whose fare was paid as well as transfer of men in the ordinary way where the government did not pay.
While I am on this subject I may say that we have done a great deal in the matter of taking care of what the hon. member for Cape Breton South describes as "pockets of unemployment", by seeing to it that through the clearance system of the national employment service the unemployed persons are, to use technical jargon "exposted to jobs". That is the technical phrase they use. Once a fellow has been to a university he sometimes uses peculiar expressions.
Where the placement necessitates a long journey we often supply transportation under 
one of two methods: first, where we can, we have the employer provide the transportation on a refundable basis; and secondly where this is not possible, the government itself provides the transportation.
Some of the places where the government supplies transportation are those my hon. friend mentioned, namely, in the maritimes, Halifax, Cape Breton, New Glasgow and Pictou, and during the winter we arranged a movement from Vancouver city to eastern Canada.
Many transfers were arranged where the companies paid the fare. For example, the Ontario Hydro moved a large number of men, and a number of lumber companies advanced fares.
The plans developed for transferring men from one part of the country to another have worked out wonderfully well and have resulted in alleviating the unemployment situation in their home areas. The actual number moved from the maritimes at government expense was 2,644. During the winter the movement slowed down.
Some questions were asked in regard to displaced persons. First of all, I should like to say that there is a very close arrangement with the immigration department. When employers offer to engage displaced persons their statement is checked to make sure that the workers are not available in Canada, and if in the opinion of the national employment service there is no need to bring people from the displaced persons camps, that application is not accepted. We insist on prevailing wages being paid, and see to it that the working conditions are good, that housing is available, and that the charge for board is not unreasonable.
After the men or women are placed, we have a follow-up system through the employment service, and periodically visits are made to see that there is no difficulty.
As I stated, we make periodical inspections and in addition where there is any complaint from either the employer or the employee we check at once, and occasionally we do make transfers. In other words, a person is not required to stay with an employer if he finds conditions unacceptable.
Some question was raised as to the type of undertaking. We have not provided for a contract; we have adopted the plan put into effect by the British government, which is that the displaced person makes application to come to Canada, and in doing so agrees to follow the line of work provided for him by the Minister of Labour for a stated period, usually one year. Our experience has been that the D.P.'s themselves are appreciative of the fact that they have been brought to Canada, and on the whole they are quite willingly carrying out their undertaking. On the other hand we have had cases where attempts have been made to find ways and means of getting into other occupations. For example, two girls who were placed with a hospital in Saint John thought it would be a good idea to leave Saint John and go to the United States. Of course when they were discovered in the United States they got into trouble and were returned.
We do impress on the D.P.'s that they have an obligation, and we do require them to live up to it as far as we can. I must say that in this the national employment service has been remarkably successful. Never before has greater care been taken in arranging a movement of workers to this country, and I must say to hon. members that I am sometimes astounded at the success we have had. As I said last night, hundreds of letters of approval and appreciation have been received from the D.P.'s themselves and from employers. The Ontario hydro-and this is significant, Mr. Chairman-has taken sixteen hundred D.P.'s and has had only one man leave. I do not know of a smaller turnover in any undertaking in this country, and I think it reflects credit both on those in charge of the industry and on the men themselves. As I stated last night, there is nothing to prevent any of these D.P.'s from joining any organization they wish to. In passing I might say that they are carefully screened. We do not want any communists, and so long as I am in control of this movement no communist will knowingly be allowed to enter Canada from Europe. Let that be clearly understood.

speechtext: Or nazis either.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP LABOUR GOVERNMENT OF CANADA
speechtext: Or nazis either. There is a big enough place for those fellows to play elsewhere, without upsetting our economy in Canada. I would be remiss in my duty if I failed to express our appreciation of the great help we have had from the Y.W.C.A., the Catholic Women's League, the Canadian Red Cross, provincial educational institutions, the Sisters of Service and church organizations. I wish to pay tribute to the great assistance that has been rendered by all these organizations, particularly in the movement of young girls from displaced persons' camps in Europe. It is a difficult thing to move large groups of young girls from Europe to a strange land, and every precaution is taken to see that they are well taken care of and placed in what we consider to be good homes in this country.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South also mentioned pockets of unemployment. It is true that such pockets do develop in every
Supply-Labour

country, and Canada is no exception. In transferring unemployed persons to other places, two methods are followed with regard to transportation costs. In some cases the employer advances the fares; in others the government pays the fares. This plan has worked wonderfully well and thousands of men and women are moved through the agency of the national employment service every month.
The arrangement in regard to the fares of unemployed people from Halifax, Sydney and Cape Breton has not been cancelled, and I regret if I gave any such impression. The operation has continued since it was first started in 1947. The total number moved to date is approximately 2,700. Those are cases where the government paid the fare. Speaking from memory last night I said the number was 2,800. It is not to be expected that married men will be too ready to leave their homes, and there has not been as great a movement as might have developed but for this fact. Usually we can find housing in the new location for single men but not for families.
Never before has better service been given the workers of Canada in the matter of finding them suitable jobs. I firmly believe that the high level of employment in Canada is due in no small measure to the fact that we now have in Canada a national employment service, which is giving excellent service to employees and employers alike. In the year 1947 our various offices placed 769,849 persons -I said around 700,000 last night, speaking from memory-which is evidence that both employers and employees are using the service.

I should like to say this if I might, and then I am through. I think my hon. friend knows my views about labour organizations, and I express this one frankly. I think the proper place in which to correct an organization is on the inside, not on the outside. If you do not like the policy that has been followed by your officers, the proper thing to do is to clean up on the inside. Political parties have to do that, and you have to do it in your family; but you should not go out and talk about it.
I was always taught-and I am a great believer in the rule that the simple things govern the destiny of our civilization-that a family row should stay inside the family and should not be carried out to the street. That is a rule in which I believe, particularly with regard to labour negotiations. The less said until you get negotiations under way, the better. People being as suspicious as they are by nature, the less said publicly, the more chance you have of settling a dispute. I know people like to see their names in the newspapers. I suppose that is only natural. But in labour negotiations, when people are suspicious and hang on to little phrases and expressions of opinion, the less said the better, until a settlement has been reached. I think you can have a brass band when the matter is settled, and it is then all right to go to our newspaper friends and say, "Here is the settlement; three cheers for the red, white and blue". That is a point I should like cleared up. P.C. 1003 was accepted by the Ontario government and made applicable to all industry in this province. I have to take my advice on questions of law from the justice department. In a recent case in my hon. friend's province, the supreme court definitely stated, if my memory serves me correctly, that under the British North America Act the provincial government has not power to delegate authority to the federal government. I forget the name of the case, but I presume that point will be argued before the Supreme Court of Canada. In Saskatchewan a couple of years ago- and I am not offering any criticism, because Mr. Williams, the minister of labour there, is a personal friend-they had a strike at a box factory in Prince Albert. I am just wondering what would have happened in this house if I had risen and expressed my opinion on that dispute.
Speaking internationally, it is my belief that this world would be a better place if people would stay in their own back yards. That is a sound principle to apply to any kind of legislation. The world would be a better place today if some of the international crackpots were out of the way; and if there were more people with some degree of common sense,

like my hon. friend the member for Cape Breton South, the world would be a happier place in which to live. Naturally my sympathies are with the men engaged in labour-and I see the hon. member for Vancouver East is ready to deliver a blast. Frankly, however, we cannot become involved in the jurisdiction of the provinces. In Quebec there is a premier who believes in the principle of provincial rights, and we have that same condition right across Canada. And the only place-

That is the principle I have in mind. Certainly I do not intend to ask the minister to intervene in matters over which he has no jurisdiction. I understand clearly the distinction between the jurisdiction of the federal Minister of Labour and the respective jurisdictions of the ministers of labour of the provinces. I suggest that, instead of our waiting until a strike takes place, some action should be taken. For instance, the federal minister has jurisdiction over the railways, if we wish to discuss a case in point. The minister and his department endeavour to do all kinds of things before conditions reach a stage where settlement becomes increasingly difficult. I wish that in other phases of activity a similar disposition would be shown by those charged with the responsibility of settling labour disputes. Instead of waiting until people's minds become inflamed, I wish they would step in a little earlier and offer some help.
I do not think it is good policy to stay in your own back yard when you can render some assistance to your neighbour in clearing up some dirt in his back yard. I believe that in these questions of labour relations we can be neighbours. After my experience in labour relations, I am positive we can render considerable service and consequently reduce the enormous costs involved, instead of making it necessary to go through protracted negotiations and conciliations which, in the final analysis, are recommendations only and the
decision as to whether one or other of the parties will accept the final finding of the board of conciliation is still left.
I offer this only as a suggestion in the light of my personal experience in these matters. If the minister does not wish to accept what I have said as useful information, that is his privilege. I offer it, however, as one who, though new in the house, is old in this phase of industrial relations.
