speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before I speak to this item, there are a few matters of general interest I should like to mention. May I first extend my congratulations and best wishes to the newly appointed Minister of Fisheries from British Columbia. For many long years British Columbia has been asking for representation in the fisheries department. It has been long held by those in the east that the minister holding that portfolio should come from the maritimes, even though British Columbia produces over 50 per cent of the fish and fish products produced in Canada. When the maritimes are mentioned it means one, two or three provinces, but British Columbia alone produces 50 per cent of all the fisheries of Canada, including those in inland waters. Hence we felt that we had a good case for recognition. I am therefore glad to say that at long last we have been given that recognition, and I wish the new minister every success in his new duties.
I should like to place before the department one particular matter which I think should receive serious consideration by the minister after the session is over. I refer to proposed power development in British Columbia which if carried out as proposed will destroy two-thirds of the sockeye salmon run on the Fraser river. On March 27 an announcement was made in the press that a big aluminum plant would be established in British Columbia. The production of aluminum, it appears, requires electric power.
It is not generally known, although it is to members from British Columbia, that the government of British Columbia has made a complete survey of the potential water powers of that province. The latest bulletin which I hold in my hand was issued by the water powers branch of the provincial government in 1938. Any hon. member who is interested can get a copy which contains very complete maps and graphs showing the potential hydropower development.
Supply-Fisheries

I am speaking now more particularly as a member of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission. We who are interested in fisheries, particularly those of the Fraser river, have for some time viewed with alarm the possible development of hydroelectric power in British Columbia. That alarm is caused by what took place in the United States. In spite of the fish ladders which were constructed on the Columbia river at a cost of many millions, the fact is, despite all the wonderful statistics published by the United States fisheries department, salmon fishing on the Columbia river is gradually going down.
True, the fish ladders which were constructed have permitted the salmon to get up over the dams to reach the spawning beds; but, although the authorities have tried for twelve years, no one has yet discovered how to bring the little fingerlings down over the dams, and that is the crux of the entire situation. Fingerlings bj' the millions are unable to negotiate the large falls. They have protected them to a certain extent in going through the turbines, but investigation has shown that millions of the fingerlings die, or are lost when migrating down stream over the dams.
In the past, the fisheries department, no matter under what government, has not taken any great interest in .what happens or might happen to the fish after dams have been built. I should like to cite one instance. The British Columbia .power company erected a hydroelectric plant on the Alouette river to supply Vancouver and other places with electricity. The entire river was dried up, and today it serves no purpose so far as the salmon fisheries are concerned.
The press report which I hold in my hand states that the Aluminum company are about to proceed to construct an electric .power plant on Chilko lake. Most of the projects set out in the book which I hold in my hand have in mind the construction of dams, but this .project indicates that something new is to be done. The water from the lake is to be taken away by means of flume or tunnel and dropped into another lake. Chilko lake by the way .produces about two-thirds of the sockeye salmon in the Fraser river.
They would take the water from the lake and perhaps take it into Bute inlet. I say "perhaps," because one or two different schemes are outlined. They are going to utilize the water from the lake for the development of electric power. That water will be taken from .the Fraser river entirely and the lake drained or used. Sockeye salmon will be prevented from going to Chilko lake, first by the dam at the inlet to the lake and, second, by the fact that the water from

the lake is to be drained off for the development of power and diverted on to the sea.
In 1913, before the disaster which occurred, at Hell's Gate, an estimated 2,500,000 cases of salmon were produced from the sockeye going up the Fraser river. If one takes an average of ten salmon to a case that equals 25,000,000 salmon. We estimate that in those days at least 20,000,000 salmon went up the Fraser and its various tributaries to spawn.
Then the disaster at Hell's Gate occurred, but I do not intend to go into that at the moment. Fish ladders have been constructed, there by the two governments, the government of the United States and the government of Canada. Last year 3,000,000 sockeye were counted going up to the spawning beds, while 6,000,000 were caught by the fishermen of the United States and Canada. When you consider the difference between the run of 1947 and that of 1913 you will understand why the members bf the commission are so much alarmed, and perturbed over this projected industry.
' We are not arguing as members of the commission that there should not be any development of hydroelectric power from the waters of British Columbia, but we do point out respectfully to both the provincial government and the industrialists that in the interior of British Columbia there are water areas which could be utilized for the development of power and to which no salmon go. We have made a complete survey of the lakes and rivers of British Columbia and can show by our charts, maps and data the lakes and rivers which .produce salmon and also those which do not produce .any salmon.
Before projects such as the one which I have mentioned are carried out-and this one would destroy two-thirds of the sockeye run of the Fraser river-we say that these water areas should be examined. As it is now, without any consultation with the federal Department of Fisheries or the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission, projects detrimental to the fishing industry on the Fraser river and its tributary streams and lakes are commenced, or proposed.
I have stated on many occasions that the provincial authorities do not look very kindly on the fisheries of the Fraser river. They are power-minded, and I use that phrase in a double sense, meaning hydroelectric power, and second, the power of complete control over these rivers. Fisheries come, of course, under the dominion government, and the provincial authorities are therefore not as much interested in salmon as they should be. Although we have approached the provincial government

Supply-Fisheries
on many occasions and have had assurances from at least two premiers and their deputies; yet when industrialists come along and ask for the right to construct dams and go ahead with power projects they are given every assurance that their applications will be granted, and neither the dominion Department of Fisheries nor the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission is made aware of what they are doing.
They had the same trouble in the state of Washington, and the federal authorities at Washington, D.C., took the matter up with the provincial authorities of Washington state, whose authority compares with the province of British Columbia. On this side of the line we call them provinces, and on the other side of the line they call them states. The federal authorities persuaded the Washington state authorities to pass a statute, a part of which I am going to read, and I suggest to the Minister of Fisheries that he take serious note of this and between now and next session take this matter up with the provincial government of British Columbia with a view to their passing similar legislation.
The act passed by the state of Washington provided:
In the event that any person, firm, corporation or government agency desires to construct any form of hydraulic project or other project that will use, divert, obstruct or change the natural flow or bed of any river or stream or that will utilize any of the waters of the state or materials from the stream beds, such person, firm, corporation or government agency shall submit to the department of fisheries and the department of game full plans and specifications of their proposed construction or work, complete plans and specifications for the proper protection of fish life in connection therewith, the approximate date when such construction or work is to commence and shall secure the written approval of the director of game.
I say to the Minister of Fisheries in all kindness that it is time that we had some such protection in Canadian laws. As it is now, the only protection we have is contained in section 20 of the Fisheries Act, which reads;
Every slide, dam or other obstruction across or in any stream where the minister determines it to be necessary for the public interest that a fishpass should exist, shall be provided by the owner or occupier with a durable and efficient fishway, or canal around the slide, dam or other obstruction . . .
I shall not take time to read the whole of the section, but I draw the minister's attention to this section 20 of the Fisheries Act and point out to him respectfully that it is no protection whatsoever to our fishing industry, because when you come to examine it carefully you find that no action can be taken until the dam is actually constructed, in which case the
run of fish for that year may be completely wiped out before any action can be taken by the dominion government.
I am not going to thresh old history. I merely point out that on one of the tributaries of the Fraser, the Alouette, a dam was built for the development of power and it wiped out a valuable salmon run which before had gone up the Alouette river.
I am greatly concerned, and I know the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission is also greatly concerned in regard to the project I have mentioned, and I say in all seriousness to the minister that no time should be lost after the session in making representations to the provincial government, first of all, to find out whether it is true; second, to find out whether permission has been granted; and third, to request that before any licence is granted the whole fisheries industry, and particularly that of the sockeye salmon industry, be examined as to the possible effects upon it by the construction of the dam, provided that a licence is granted by the provincial government to proceed with the project. I am not going to labour the point further, but I thought I would take a few minutes to impress upon the minister the seriousness of the matter, because action is necessary now before the project is further proceeded with.
There are one or two other matters I wish to place before the minister for his consideration after the end of the session. First, I would suggest that we have a fisheries representative in the external affairs department of the government. In the United States, when their minister of external affairs is dealing with nationals of other countries, a fisheries expert sits in to advise and is thereby enabled to give some protection to the fisheries of the United States. The time has long since passed in this country when we should have such an official attached to the Department of External Affairs.	i
In support of what I urge, let me recall what happened regarding Newfoundland and Great Britain. I do not know who fell down on the job, but I know that almost since confederation Canada has been the chief supplier of salt cod to Italy and various other countries on the continent of Europe. We understand that there is at the present time a dearth of United States currency in Great Britain, which is hampering her trade to quite an extent, but some time ago the news came out that Great Britain had made United States funds available to Newfoundland to enable her to capture our market for salt cod in Italy and other countries. Something like nine thousand tons of salt cod were sold by Newfoundland to Italy and othwr
Supply-Fisheries

countries, through Great Britain assisting Newfoundland with United States dollars. Had we had at that time a fisheries expert attached to the Department of External Affairs, a deal of that kind might not have been allowed to go through.
My fourth point is this. There should be closer co-operation between the department and the fisheries research board. Two years ago I made what was interpreted as a violent attack in this connection. I did so knowingly, because I felt that the fisheries research department had to be shaken up in some way. I am not going to indulge in any carping criticism, but I might mention that between sessions I visited the station at Nanaimo, and I must say there is need for closer co-operation between the minister's department and the officials of the fisheries research board. The first step has been taken. We have one officer attached to the board, but that does not establish sufficiently close co-operation.
There is another matter which I would ask the minister to consider between now and the next session, and that is off-shore fisheries. Off the coast of Vancouver island, beyond the three-mile limit, the nationals of the United States and Canada are fishing, and from reports reaching me I think it is safe to say that the fisheries close to Vancouver island are being depleted. It is true they are outside the three-mile limit, but the United States has taken action to protect its own nationals who fish beyond the three-mile limit off United States territory. We cannot sit idly by and see our off-shore fisheries depleted by nationals of other countries.
May I also bring to the minister's notice the importance of a decision with regard to Hecate strait. I made a speech on this subject last year and I do not intend to repeat it on this occasion, but Hecate strait was designated as Canadian waters many years ago. In fact Canadian or government vessels have in past years chased off American boats. Looking to the future, I suggest that steps be taken to proclaim Hecate strait Canadian waters. I point out that if we allow United States fishermen to fish in those waters with impunity there is nothing to hinder vessels from Japan and Soviet Russia from entering the waters and depleting them, and when they do so we shall find ourselves in some difficulties if we try to chase them off. They will reply that Americans had been fishing there.
I suggest also to the minister that some thought be given to a revision of the Fisheries Act. I do not know how many years it is since the act was revised, but in between sessions the minister should look that question

over with his officials. If he does, I think he will find that my suggestion that the act be reviewed as soon as possible is a good one, and, if acted upon, it would be a step in the right direction.
One further remark I wish to make has reference to the dyeing of seal furs. I could take up all these matters under the several items as they came up, but I think it might be better for me to deal with them all at the same time. That would save time. In connection with the dyeing of seal furs, I notice that there is an estimate of $550,000. That matter was debated when the treaty came before the house, but I would suggest that steps should be taken, even if money has to be spent, for the setting up of a dyeing establishment in British Columbia.
After all, no province except British Columbia, if you get down to the morals of the thing, can claim any of the money we receive from the United States on account of the sale of these furs. Bear in mind that the people of British Columbia had an industry there. It is true they were hunting seals in open waters, and at some other time I shall give the history of that. At the moment I simply point out that we in British Columbia have a moral right to the moneys obtained from these furs, because it was British Columbia fishermen who were put out of business when the treaty went through. It affected no other fishermen in Canada. Some thought should be given to this matter, and I am confident that the minister will look into it with a view to establishing an industry in the dyeing of these furs.
It cannot all be done m one year, because the process is a secret one; but why should we send our furs either to St. Louis or to Great Britain? When we investigate the establishment of industries, I think it will be readily agreed that this is one industry that belongs to British Columbia. I am willing to debate that with any member of the committee.
I close by again wishing the minister every success in his new position.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. MAYHEW (Minister of Fisheries) :
speechtext:
I will try to answer some of the questions the hon. member has put to me in so kindly and constructive a manner. I wish to thank him for the job he has been doing and for the way in which he has made his presentation to me.
As regards the Chilko lake power plant of the Aluminum Company of Canada, that is a new development. At the present time it is really not on paper. It is talked of, but I do not mean to say it is not a possibility or even

Supply-Fisheries
a probability, though it is quite a new venture. I assure my hon. friend that it will receive the immediate attention of the department; in fact, it has already received attention. Further attention will be given it, and as I shall be going to the west coast soon I will take that occasion to discuss the matter with the provincial government.
It is quite true that our legislation would enable us to tell anyone developing power plants on any of our rivers that he must provide fish ladders. The hon. member for New Westminster is quite right. At the same time, we would be a little late with our present legislation and we shall have to take that into consideration.
The hon. member referred to the fisheries department being represented with external affairs, and I can assure him that there has been the closest possible liaison between the two departments. That will be continued. The Department of Fisheries is one department that is greatly concerned with what goes on in our relations with our neighbours, and I assure the committee that that is the case at the present time.
As regards the Newfoundland and United Kingdom deal on cod fish, that is an offer by the United Kingdom to the Newfoundland government. It is one that we would have no control over; but we can negotiate and are negotiating with the United Kingdom government, seeking to be put in the same position as the government of Newfoundland in the matter of fish.
So far as the liaison with the research board is concerned, we have already representatives on that board in the persons of Doctor Needier and Mr. Sutherland, and) another official whom we expect on our staff very shortly, Doctor Pritchard. So that that is taken care of.
As regards the curing of fur seals at the present time, that is done in the United States in St. Louis and at Martin's in London. Apparently they are the only people who have the knowledge necessary to cure these seal skins. It is not simply a question of building a plant; you must get the technical knowledge to do the curing when the plant is established. That may be obtainable in some form or another. These seal skins are worth $20 per skin more with the St. Louis process than they are with the process in England. This matter must be given considerable study before we would embark on the building of a plant, but all the items the hon. member has brought to my attention will receive consideration.
The hon. member referred to the Fisheries Act. I have inquired about that, and I find that it has been some time since the act was 5849-373
really reviewed. I have asked the legal adviser to have a look at it to see what changes, if any, need to be made.

As representing the constituency adjacent to that represented by the minister, I offer him my congratulations on his appointment as Minister of Fisheries. I am quite certain that he will bring the full measure of his ability and his long experience to the department, and I express the hope that he may hold that appointment for the rest of his parliamentary career.
I should like to ask one question which concerns fisheries in the northern part of our province. The international boundary between British Columbia and Alaska runs from a point northwest of Prince Rupert due west to the southern end of Prince of Wales island, known as Point Muzon. I was rather disturbed the other day when the Minister of Mines and Resources said quite recently consideration had been given on a technical level with regard to the changing of that international boundary. If that international boundary is moved further south-and I presume that is the direction in which it is intended to make any change-our valuable salmon-halibut fisheries in the Dixon entrance and perhaps in Hecate strait will be seriously interfered with. It is a matter of tremendous importance to the fishing industry. I wish the minister would tell us how far those negotiations with the United States have gone for the changing of the boundary, to which the Minister of Mines and Resources referred at page 5684 of Hansard of June 22 of this year.

Preliminary steps have been taken with the Department of External Affairs, objecting to any change in boundary that would alter the fishing grounds of Canada. It has only been preliminary, but I assure the hon. member for Nanaimo that is going on and will be prosecuted to the limit of our ability.
Did I hear the minister say that his department was objecting to any changes?
Any changes that would be detrimental to the fishing industry of Canada.
If the boundary were moved farther south, thus giving a larger share of those northern waters to the United States, surely that would be detrimental to the fishing industry of Canada, would it not?

I would naturally think anything that lessens our area at all would be detrimental. But the matter is under study
Supply-Fisheries

at the preseat time and has beea taken up with the Department of External Affaire.

The minister cannot give us any further information on the subject? It is one of national importance as well as one of importance to the fishing industry. Obviously some sort of consideration is being given at the present time to changing the international boundary of Canada. I think the people of this country are entitled to know what is behind this move. Why should Canada desire at this time-if she does so desire-a change to be made? This is something that just cannot be passed over without some explanation from the government. I wish the minister would explain as fully as he possibly can how far these negotiations have gone, what are the proposals which have been made either by Canada or the United States and how they will affect the fishing industry of Canada. It is something about which the people of Canada should be informed. It is something in which the fishing industry of British Columbia would be most vitally concerned.

I am afraid there is nothing more that I can add to what I have said. Negotiations are going on. The province of British Columbia has also been brought into the discussion, and the interests of Canada will be taken care of.
At whose initance were those negotiations started?
It was referred to us by external affairs, so that I imagine it started in the Department of External Affairs. Probably the hon. member's question would be better directed to that department.
I mean, by which country were negotiations started? Is it a change desired by Canada or a change desired by the United States?
I cannot answer that at the present time.

The Minister of Mines and Resources used the expression "until quite recently, at the technical level." I presume that the negotiations have now moved forward from the technical level to the cabinet level, if the matter has been referred by one department to another.
It is still on the technical level, so far as I know. It has not been on the cabinet level yet.

As a member from the east coast, I should like to start by saying a word of welcome to the new Minister of Fisheries. We regard it as a fitting tribute to
fMr. Mayhew.]
the great industry on the west coast that, after all these years, they should finally have their first Minister of Fisheries. We also feel that they have the night man in the job; one who has had a significant and successful career in industry and who brings a great deal of experience to the portfolio. I should also like to say that we were pleased about the appointment of the parliamentary assistant, the hon. member for Prince. We feel that in the balance between east and west the government has a strong combination that will produce.
And take care of all in between.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I should like for just a fe*y moments again to bring to the attention of the committee some of the problems which are facing commercial fishermen. The fishing industry has always to struggle to fit into any economic pattern and present-day conditions present real problems. I think the difficulty has greater emphasis on the east coast, but fishermen the country over usually feel that they are in an orphan industry.
When the national income is high, people purchase highnpriced foods and eat fish far too seldom. When the national economy is tight, there is not enough money to pay a reasonable price for fish, with the result that the fisherman suffers again. It is in the nature of a marginal industry; it reacts first to an economic let-down and benefits last from an upswing.
It is fully realized that if Canadians would eat more fish, the industry would be much healthier, and so would our Canadian citizens. But until the internal consumption goes up quite materially, we shall have to depend to a large extent on foreign markets, where we are at the mercy of various governments. Our national consumption of fish is still far and away below our national production.
With the price of meat high, a solution of part of our cost of living worries is to eat more fish and less meat. Now is the golden opportunity for the industry to make a determined attempt to expand domestic consumption; but in order to do so, it will be obliged to put on the market a good quality product. This involves a comprehensive inspection, and in this both the department and the industry 'have been making good progress. This is, however, a field for a considerable amount of further development.
In the fresh fish market our best customer is the United States. The predominant export on the east coast, apart from lobsters, is fresh fillets of cod and haddock. Much has been said of tariff concessions gained at Geneva, and we are not unmindful of the splendid

Supply-Fisheries
work done by our representatives. But the best that could be done for cod and haddock fillets was to have the outstanding tariff rate bound at what it was. In other words for our most important fresh fish product, there was no change in tariff; but we are in a little better position as a result of a revision of the quota system, whereby the United States now allocates the total quota on a quarterly basis instead of annually as heretofore. This enables us to compete on better terms with countries such as Iceland which might otherwise flood the United Staites market at one season of the year and, in so doing, use up most of the quota.
Prices of fresh fish increased during last winter to the point where fishermen could make a decent living if catches were good. As is well known, deep-sea fishermen work on a share of the catch basis; the shore fishermen, of course, earn in direct relation to the amount of fish they catch. During the winter the weather was against our fishermen and fish were scarce. In the spring and early summer, fish have been plentiful and the price has held, but the weather has been most adverse. As a result, though deep-sea schooners and draggers have done well recently, shore fishermen have not been experiencing good catches and returns have been relatively low. The lobster season in many districts was not up to average, and fishermen who count heavily on this product have suffered varying degrees of disappointment.
The salt and pickled fish branch of the industry is having its own special and serious problems. This branch depends almost entirely upon the export market in the West Indies. The ironic problem here is that, though the demand is good, the countries which wish to buy cannot do so because of a shortage of dollars. For provinces such as Nova Scotia and for industries such as fishing, which historically have looked for their prosperity to foreign trade, the impact of the present relationship between dollar and sterling countries is a heavy blow. This is a problem to which our financial experts should give their best attention.
I wish to associate myself with the remarks made by the hon. member for New Westminster, who gave a splendid presentation of the fishery problems of the west coast. He pointed out that the United Kingdom appears to be discriminating against Canada in favour of certain empire countries in the matter of dollar dealings. Recently there have been concessions on the part of the United Kingdom to certain of our competitors, which have given them an advantage over Canada in the European market. The hon. member for New 5849-373J
Westminster referred specifically, I think, to dealings with Greece. While we in Canada have no wish that anything shall be done to upset arrangements entered into with other members of the British commonwealth, the least we should expect from the mother country is to be treated on the same basis as the rest of the commonwealth with respect to an industry that is so vital to our welfare.
With regard to dry salt fish, there is a problem arising out of a United States regulation for which it is difficult to account. The regulation provides that a higher duty shall apply to fish having less than 43 per cent moisture than to fish having more than 43 per cent moisture. The continental United States market is not important to us, but the trouble is that the regulation applies to Puerto Rico, in which we are vitally interested. The rate on fish having more than 43 per cent moisture was reduced in 1922 at the request of New England fish processors, who wished to obtain cheaper fish to process and market as boneless fish. A wet fish is used for this purpose. Neither the tariff nor the differential applying at 43 per cent is of any importance to the United States or Canada when only these two countries are concerned; but the trouble is that the differential influences Puerto Rico to buy a wet or green fish at lower tariff rates, and Nova Scotia fish, having a higher moisture content, do not stand up well in warm climates. In other words, we cannot assure the quality that is so vital in international dealings, when the moisture content of our fish is high. On the other hand, Newfoundland and Labrador dried fish, with the higher moisture content, do not deteriorate so rapidly in warmer climates, with the result that Newfoundland has a decided advantage over us in this market. Then, too, when it is considered that there is no satisfactory and consistent method for determining the moisture content of dried fish, it must be concluded that the 43 per cent line of demarcation is pretty arbitrary.
This may not sound important, but I can assure the committee that it is of the greatest consequence to salt fish producers in Nova Scotia. We urge our negotiators at any future trade talks with the United States to do their best to have the differential removed. Failing that, we would urge that the moisture content at which the differential applies be increased from 43 per cent to around 50 per cent, thereby giving us a better chance to compete with Newfoundland. At a recent meeting of the banking and commerce committee, Mr. F. Homer Zwicker of Lunenburg was given an opportunity to present this case on behalf of the salt fish exporters association.
Supply-Fisheries

He was given valuable assistance by the senior hon. member for Halifax, who is a member of that committee and quite familiar with the situation, and who realizes the difficulty under which our salt fish trade is obliged to operate as a result.
The fishing industry is a hard one for all concerned. The returns to operators and fishermen alike, depend upon the amount of fish caught, export markets and our own domestic consumption, all of which are highly variable. Add the hazards, discomfiture and hardships endured in open boats in all kinds of weather, and one can well imagine that there is no other industry in which personal initiative and courage run higher. Fishermen c-annot demand and get pay raises with assured incomes as can labourers in other industries. They can only share in what they catch, and be paid only in relation to what consumers will pay for their products. Nevertheless the conditions under which deep-sea fishermen work and the returns to all types of fishermen have improved. Recently the hon. member for Cape Breton South stated that production increased by 196 per cent between 1938 and 1945, and that since the war it had gone back to about what it was in 1938. This is entirely contrary to the facts. The total value of sea fish landed in the three maritime provinces and Quebec in 1938 was $8,687,000, while in 1946 it was $34,358,000. In 1947, despite the fact that there was a strike of three months' duration, the value of the catch was $23,288,000, or almost three times what it was in 1938.
The same hon. member referred to the fisherman as the forgotten man, and pointed to his low income. It is true that returns to fishermen are not as high as the government or the industry would like to see them, and shore fishermen in particular often do not receive adequate compensation in relation to (he work they do and the hazards they take; but it is fair to look at the over-all picture. In the first five months of 1948, six schooners, picked at random, shared $997.68 per man, or very close to $200 a month. Of six drag-gers .for which I have figures for the same period, each deck hand averaged $1,255.32, or $251 a month. On some draggers the men averaged over $300 a month. In 1939 the price of cod and haddock averaged about one and a half cents a pound for the whole round fish. In 1945 the price of codfish varied from 34 cents to 4 cents, and the price of haddock from 41 cents to 5 cents. The 1948 prices to date are the same as those in 1945. Therefore, whereas the hon. member from Cape Breton South says that conditions in the fishing industry improved up to 1946 and then

receded to where they were before the war, the encouraging fact is that, with continued heavy fishing and sustained prices, it is a reasonable estimate that deep-sea fishermen will get as much or more in 1948 than they did in 1946.
The statements made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South are the sort of characteristic inaccuracies which are harmful to the industry and to the maritimes. At a recent meeting in Cherry Hill, the Rev. Fred Young, who, I understand, is a professional organizer for the C.C.F. party, discussed fishing problems. As reported from Bridgewater on May 7, the Rev. Mr. Young stated that, while the Lunenburg county fisherman is getting from three to four cents a pound for his catch, the Halifax consumer pays twenty-nine cents a pound for the same fish. He may, or may not, have been aware of a gross inaccuracy; nevertheless he is comparing unlike quantities. It is true that the fisherman is paid from 34 to 4 cents a pound for the fish in the round, whole state; but it takes about three pounds of this fish to make a pound of fillets; and it is the price of fillets which Mr. Young quotes at twenty-nine cents a pound. The spread, including processing, distribution, selling, refrigerating, and other costs is, therefore, between twelve cents and twenty-nine cents, and not between four cents and twenty-nine cents, as is used for propaganda purposes. In the same report Mr. Young continued his attempt to spread unrest in the industry by making the mysterious statement that a C.C.F. government in Canada would establish floor prices under fish, thereby lowering consumer prices and greatly increasing consumption.
As I have said before in this discussion, and on previous occasions, the shore fisherman is the man who, more than any other, works abnormally hard for uncertain returns in the face of great hazards. He is constantly running the risk of losing his boat and his gear, and at the present time there is no means whereby he can obtain insurance such as that available to registered or tonnage boats. This has been a matter of concern, and some months ago I asked the department to undertake a study with a view to determining the feasibility of initiating an insurance program with the premiums to be shared jointly by the fishermen and the government. I was pleased to learn that this matter had been raised as far back as 1931 by one of my predecessors, an outstanding Conservative member, Mr. W. G. Ernst, who later became minister of fisheries. Unfortunately, for various reasons, no plan was brought forth at that time, nor has any suitable program been worked out for the east coast to date.

Supply-Fisheries
The Department of Fisheries has assigned to the problem personnel who have given it the most searching study and have compiled comprehensive figures on losses, damage and other factors. I wish to compliment the department upon the manner in which they have applied themselves to this study and to express the hope that a plan can be formulated which will be satisfactory to the fishermen; for it would provide a vital stimulant to inshore fishing, which is that phase of the indiustry most urgently in need of support. It would enable these fishermen to operate with more confidence and would serve to provide an element of solidarity and stability, which the industry can well use.
I should like to endorse the remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster respecting his suggestion that a fisheries expert be included in the Department of External Affairs. To my mind that is a good suggestion. I believe also that we could use more men with a detailed knowledge of fisheries in the Department of Trade and Commerce.
May I repeat what I said last year with respect to the continental shelf. I believe it is time the Canadian government took some steps to extend Canadian sovereignty over those waters which normally we regard as our own home waters, namely, the waters usually embraced within the limits of the continental shelf.
In closing, may I again extend the best wishes of the east coast fisheries to the new minister, and hope that he will remain in his office for some considerable time.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to compliment the minister upon his appointment. It is good to see a Minister of Fisheries from British Columbia. I have enjoyed in the past the co-operation of the Department of Fisheries, and I have no doubt that it will continue in the future.
I have only one or two points I should like to mention at the present time. First, there is the matter of the short halibut season, and the fact that the fishermen in the Canadian halibut fleet are interested in seeing that the international halibut commission be given more power, so that the season may be spread out over a longer period of time. The purpose would be to prevent such a large mass of fish from coming in, in such a short space of time, and thus prevent a depression in the market. This short season is bad for the fishing grounds. It is hard to handle such large quantities in so short a space of time. I have no doubt that there will be some depression in fish prices, and these large quantities coming on the market will help to depress the price still
further. I would ask the department to take an interest in this matter so that such a crisis might be averted.
The suggestion by the hon. member for New Westminster in which he asks for a fisheries expert in the external affairs branch is a good one. I should like to see a little more aggressiveness on the part of Canada when we are dealing with the United States. It would seem that we take their desires at face value, but that they are slow when we ask for concessions.
Then, possibly the minister would answer the question I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other evening, namely, about fish livers. I shall not repeat my question in detail, because the minister is familiar with it.
May I speak respecting the need of proper repair equipment in northern British Columbia for patrol vessels? The department needs that equipment, and I should like to see them move from their present quarters at Dodge Cove to quarters at Seal Cove, where the Department of Transport is now located and at which point the Department of Fisheries controls one area. Those facilities are needed because the boats require constant attention in the northern waters.
Then, in the matter of research, at one time there was an office at Prince Rupert. I shall not go so far as to say that a full station should be established there; but in view of the amount of fish going through there, there should be established at least a substation at that point. I am sure if that were done it would be appreciated by the fishing industry.
Again let me say that I wish the minister a long term of office in his department.

Probably the hon. member for Skeena is aware that during the last week and at the present time the halibut commission have been holding a meeting in Ottawa, and that they have been discussing the question he has raised. They are placing their suggestions before the department. What may follow I am not now in a position to say, but I know the matter is under study.
It was suggested that there should be a representative of the fisheries department in the Department of External Affairs. I have already said that there is close liaison with that department. I think it is more important that there be a man who understands fisheries in the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I am happy to say that there is such a man there now.
May I say that I fully realize the value of promoting sales in any industry, and particularly in this one. That matter will have the closest attention. But I would point out that if you are to have sales volume you must go
Supply-Fisheries

right back to the fisherman. You must see that the fish is properly stored in his boat, that he has proper transportation facilities to get his fish to market, and that the handling, even in the smaller stores, is done in the right way. A long process must be followed to get the fish from the boat to the table, and each move is vital. I consider that the merchants in our various cities and towns are simply the agents of our fishermen.
The part this government must play is to carry out proper inspection at the different stages the fish must go through to reach the table. It is only by good merchandising that we can increase the production of this industry. So far as I possibly can do it, that will be done. As hon. members go through the estimates they w'ill find, as they stop at the different items-I hope they will not stop at every item-that large amounts are being asked for to carry on research and inspection work, the very things that I have just said we should try do to.
At the present time we have in the department a staff of capable young men who were brought there by the late Mr. Bridges when he was minister. We are beginning to feel the results of his work in this department. I am sure that with the energy and enthusiasm of our departmental officials we can go on to develop this industry.
I had intended making some lengthy remarks, but other arguments broke in and I shall not go on with them at the present time. However I want to say that I am happy to have as my parliamentary assistant the hon. member for Prince. He is from The Island, and with the minister being from another island on the Pacific I think we shall be able to achieve results.

I had intended to confine my remarks to one or two later items, but the remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster on the Chilko lake situation brings me to my feet at this time for an obvious reason. Chilko lake and Bute inlet are in my riding, so that we immediately have that conflict of interest between power development and the fishing industry.
Chilko lake development is one of the most unusual in British Columbia, or for that matter in Canada. As hon. members know, the interior of British Columbia is cut off from the coast by the great barrier of the coast range. The great watershed of the Fraser river is to the east of that range. Some 150 miles north of Vancouver a great fjord, Bute inlet, cuts the range. On the other side of the last mountain between the height of Bute inlet and the interior of British Columbia lies one of the

largest lakes in British Columbia, Chilko lake. This lake is at an elevation of almost 3,000 feet.
Normally the waters of that lake find an outlet through the 400 miles of the Fraser river to the sea. The proposal is to drive a tunnel through this one mountain and tap this tremendous volume of water which lies at this great height of 3,000 feet. Normally such a power development would be used to send power to Vancouver and New Westminster, but because of the mountainous nature of the country the only way in which the power can be used is to use it normally. That is why there has been no development of that site until now. It would take an industry like the Aluminum Company of Canada to make proper use of that power.
Is the reason why power could not be transmitted the high cost of constructing transmission lines?

The reason is the whole coast mountain range with its long fjords cutting across. This would require a land1 line of at least 2,000 miles to reach Vancouver. The result is that the power must be used locally by locating a power plant at the head of this long fjord.
As the hon. member for New Westminster properly said, this is one of the great tributaries of the Fraser river, and if all that water is diverted into Bute inlet it will have a serious effect, not only on the main body of the Fraser but on its tributaries. As a result, the great salmon run in the Fraser river will be seriously injured. I think between these two extremes is a type of development which will permit a flow of water out of the lake as well as allowing salmon to come in to spawn and the fingerlings to get out.
One point brought out by the hon. member was an excellent one, the fact that this must be done now. Unfortunately, until now the various provincial governments have paid little attention to the value of our streams as salmon streams. The Aluminum Company of Canada is spending $1,000,000 on surveys in that area and, unless immediate action is taken, it will be too late. One of the first tasks of our new British Columbia minister of fisheries should be to protect the salmon industry's interests in lake Chilko.
Another interesting point arises here, the flood situation. I am quite sure the hon. member for Fraser Valley will welcome this development, because the siphoning off of this great amount of water would certainly tend to reduce the flood threat on the Fraser river during the spring. This brings up once

Supply-Fisheries
more the point which the hon. member for New Westminster emphasized in his capacity as a member of the international salmon commission. This great Fraser river is not just a salmon stream or a power stream; it must be regarded as a stream in which flood control, power development and the salmon interests all play a part.
Perhaps this is the 'time to mention that the fisheries department has been instrumental in creating a new industry of tuna fishing on the Pacific coast. This type of fishing has been carried on extensively in recent years in Mexico and California, and lately some of out fishermen have been venturing out farther and farther from shore to engage in this type of fishing. The Department of Fisheries has provided great assistance in furnishing a pilot boat for our fishermen.
There is being developed on the west coast still another new industry in which I believe one of our colleagues is interested. I do not know whether the whaling industry can be called a fishing industry. When industries are started in eastern Canada they are quite often helped with subsidies, and even when they get going there seems 'to be a tendency to continue to pay those subsidies. T)f this whaling industry should have a difficult time in its first year of operations I hope the fisheries department will remember the assistance they have given and are still giving in these estimates to various kinds of fisheries on the eastern coast.
My last point is in connection with another form of assistance of which our west coast fishermen are badly in need. I intend to speak of it at some length on the estimates of the Minister of Public Works, and that is why I am particularly pleased that we have a -British Columbian as Minister of Fisheries, one who comes not only from British Columbia but from the coast, and one who, as a private member, pleaded hard with the Minister of Public Works to obtain for the fishermen on the Pacific coast a little dredging for their harbours, fishing floats, breakwaters and so forth, which this country so readily provides for the eastern provinces. I intend to deal with that at some length on the appropriate estimates, but just now I would recall to the Minister of Fisheries his own difficulties as a private member in obtaining fishing floats for Victoria and assure him that, though he now has our solid support, he will have our vociferous support if he will go as hard after the Minister of Public Works in his ministerial capacity as he did as a private member.

herring, but we can use our facilities in processing them into meal and oil to make it a satisfactory operation.
With the money that is now available to the minister through the fisheries prices support board, I trust that he will give a great deal of thought to the opportunity he now has of making fish available to the housewives all over this country. Never before was there a time when the price of beef and other meats was so high. It is the minister's golden opportunity to make fish with its valuable protein content so attractive to the housewives of Canada that we shall have a vastly greater sale of fish.
The fisheries prices support board purchased 190,000 cases of chicken haddie from the eastern coast. I believe that is all right. The only difficulty, it seems to me, is that nobody knows what to do with this chicken haddie. I do not know whether the minister has ever purchased any for his own use; but I have done some baching myself, and I know it is an excellent pack of nice white meat, wholesome and appetizing in appearance, but I have never met anybody in Canada who knew how to cook it into a tasty dish. If some spices or smoke were added to it, it would be a worthwhile product, and I would urge the minister to encourage the fisheries prices support board to do something to popularize this excellent food.
Take salt cod. The minister knows that to maritimers it is the finest food produced' in Canada. It is an excellent product. It comes packed in a wooden box and is not in itself unattractive, but not ten per cent of the housewives in this country have any idea how to cook it properly and serve it to their families, although there is no finer food produced in Canada. There is never an opportunity for maritime members to purchase a salt fish cake. Even the chef in the restaurant does not know how to cook it, and if a chef like that does not know, it is not likely that our housewives would know any better how to cook it.
I would also suggest that the minister ask the fisheries prices support board to go out and spend some money in providing freight cars to bring our fish from the coasts to markets all across Canada. The fisheries research board has been doing some work in that direction in co-operation with the railroads, although I do not think the railroads have been as co-operative as they might have been. I would ask the minister to set aside sufficient money to equip two experimental cars with their own diesel-engine operated low-temperature refrigerating equipment to bring our Pacific coast and eastern coast fish into central Canada in first-class condition. I bring that 
to his attention particularly, because a little while- ago in the parliamentary restaurant I had some fresh halibut from the Pacific coast and it tasted as if it had just come out of the sea. One week afterwards I ordered it again and it was like eating a piece of cotton batting. That was merely because it had not been properly refrigerated.
Progress reported.
