speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The committee is considering item 95, fisheries.

Mr. Chairman, prior to the adjournment of the debate at six o'clock I had what might be termed a rather lefthanded compliment paid me by the Minister of Public Works when he said that if I started to speak he would tell the Chairman not to look at the clock. I took that to mean that he wanted me to be brief. I know that brevity is golden; but at the same time, when we are dealing with these fisheries estimates, I for one will not allow them to go through en bloc just for the purpose of accommodating some hon. members who wish to get home a little earlier to their constituencies.
The fisheries are an important item and we should look carefully into the estimates for them. Even if we have to spend an extra day or so here, what does it matter. I challenge any member of this house on either side to present a better record than mine in attendance in the chamber or in days absent during the session. For that reason I for one am not going to be brushed off too hurriedly in the consideration of these estimates.
I have noticed that on many occasions in the discussion of fisheries I have found it necessary to congratulate a new minister, for the simple reason that so many hon. gentle-

Supply-Fisheries
men have occupied that portfolio. The different ministers of fisheries have been excellent men, but I do not believe that the government has given them its best support. The men in that department are able men, and even if they do not get the fullest support of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of National Revenue, they carry on and do a splendid job.
I have spoken several times on the fisheries of Canada, especially from the standpoint of my own province; and, as I have said, I have had occasion to congratulate a number of ministers directing that department even in my short time in this house. Altogether I have congratulated nine of them, and now I congratulate the new minister from British Columbia who occupies that important position. I hope that in the near-to-hand shuffle of cabinet ministers which will take place again, he will not be shuffled into some other department. In the last four months we have had four or five ministers in the department. That is not fair to the hon. gentlemen who fill the portfolio, nor is it fair to the fishing industry as a whole.
While congratulating the minister, I wish to extend my felicitations to his parliamentary assistant, who represents the constituency of Prince, which is adjacent to my own constituency of Queens. I hope that in the position he now holds he will give his very best to the fisheries of the maritime provinces in particular and generally to the industry throughout Canada. I might also hold out this hope for him, as I have seen it expressed already in the press, that in the coming cabinet shuffle which may take place in the next month he will find himself in the musical chair occupying the portfolio of Minister of Fisheries if a shuffle is made again of the present minister.
I will not say very much more about these two newly appointed hon. gentlemen, but I hope they will spend their energies and devote their abilities entirely to the fisheries of the maritimes and generally, of course, to those of Canada as a whole. In the maritimes at the present time our second primary industry is not what it should be. We are up against many difficulties.
The department has found it difficult this year to get a market for certain of our canned and processed fish. I shall deal with that later on, because I have a question or two which I wish to ask the minister.
This debate was opened by the hon. member for New Westminster, and rightly so. Who could introduce a debate on fisheries more capably than or even as well as the hon. member for New Westminster? I have heard him on many occasions and I am always glad to
listen to him. I say that for many reasons; for one thing his accent, and for another, his knowledge of our fisheries in general and particularly his knowledge of the industry in his own province of British Columbia. I doubt whether there is any other man in this house who can hold a candle to him in that regard. Another reason for which I admire him-I cannot enumerate them all-is the way in which he boosts the fisheries of British Columbia. He is just as good in that respect as he is in playing the bagpipes, and that is an accomplishment. At one time I was hoping that I would be able to congratulate the hon. member for New Westminster, but his sojourn as parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Fisheries was short lived; I do not know whether it was two days or two weeks. However, he is still occupying an important position as parliamentary assistant to another minister.
When the hon. member for New Westminster was speaking on fisheries, he spoke as if there was only one area of fishing in Canada. We have three great fishing areas, namely the west coast-British Columbia in particular-the inland fisheries and the maritime fisheries. We must all agree on this. The fish products from those three areas are the best in the world. The fish from nowhere else can hold even second place to those taken from the west coast, inland and maritime fisheries. However I think all will agree with me when I say the maritime fish are the best fish. We may not have the quantity, but, of all the fish in the world ours are the de luxe food from the briny seas. We have such fish as lobsters, scallops, oysters and mackerel-
Suckers.

That is the taxpayer.
Mr. MoLURE: -not to forget, as I did one time before, the New Brunswick salmon.
The hon. member for New Westminster, in congratulating the minister, said this appointment was British Columbia's due. In this I do not disagree with him. But in looking over the past seventeen years' history of appointments of ministers of fisheries, we find some eleven or twelve appointments; and five of those were from the maritimes, four from the inland provinces, and two from British Columbia. As I said, I do not disagree with the hon. member, because those whom he represents have a right to have a minister from the coast at certain times.
I might mention further that we in the maritimes had been promised that in 1945 we would have representation in the cabinet of this government. However, we did not get that. In 1945 I urged upon the Prime Minister
Supply-Fisheries

the fulfilment of his promise to give us a portfolio for the province, so that we would be represented in the cabinet. Now the best he gives us is a consolation prize, by making one of our members a parliamentary assistant.
And he is a good member from Prince Edward Island.

Yes, I agree with that. I have already said so. However I should have liked to have the promise fully implemented. As I said a while ago, probably in the next shuffle, which will come sooner or later, we may have representation in the cabinet.
There are many matters that I should like to bring up besides those I have already mentioned, but I shall deal with them as they come up in the estimates from time to time, and probably we can have the questions answered better in that way. I said a moment ago that our fish were excellent. What we are asking for today in our province is fishery inspection. We should have compulsory inspection in the whole of Canada. I know some hon. members agree with me in that, among whom I think would be a first-ranking member, namely the hon. member for New Westminster. I am sure he would also urge this on the Department of Fisheries and on the government. In this connection I placed a question on Hansard at page 5582. When the minister is replying I wish him to pay special attention to this question which is as follows:
Has the request of the Prince Edward Island fish canners and packers for compulsory inspection of all their canned and processed fish products been granted? If not, why not?
When the canners and packers themselves, representing the fishermen and everybody engaged in the industry, come to this department and ask for compulsory inspection, I am of the opinion that it should be granted. I hope that the minister, when he replies, will tell me and this committee that inspection for the province of Prince Edward Island, if not for the whole of Canada, will be granted as has been requested.
I shall not follow all the remarks made by the various speakers, because it would take too much time. As I said, many hon. members are in such a hurry to get away that they would be quite satisfied if I sat down immediately. However, as I said, I do not intend to be brushed aside in that way. I will take my allotted time if I want it, and then deal with some of the other matters as they come along.
Another matter to which I wish the minister to pay special attention is another request from the fisheries federation, the packers, the

fishermen, and all the different organizations in Prince Edward Island. It is this:
Will the fisheries prices support board or the Department of Fisheries endorse and support a participating advertising sales promotion plan for their canned and processed fish products from the province of Prince Edward Island ?
If not the whole of Canada. We are applying for this only for our own province.
If not, why not?
To those two questions I shall await the official answer of the minister when he replies.
Another matter about which I wish to speak is the educational service rendered by the Department of Fisheries. The educational service to our fishermen and to our fisheries should be, and it is, a matter of the greatest importance. That education should begin at the fisherman's equipment and should be carried on through all these stages of fishing, no matter of what kind, until the product is ready to go to the market. Then, when our fish start for the market we should have proper advertising; we should have proper salesmen, men who can go out and talk fish, who know the food1 value of fish, who can thus bring it before the people of Canada and find out if the consumers of Canada can be persuaded to eat, as some hon. members said when speaking this afternoon, the finest food they can eat. If they had the proper education, I believe they would start in to eat more fish. If a few pounds more were eaten by each of the inhabitants of this dominion we would find a ready market for everything our fishermen could catch.
I want to mention a matter that has to do with the Minister of Public Works. We know the best quality of fish are caught in the colder waters, the stormier seas. Consequently on the north side of our province, or any other province, where the waters are cold and the storms severe, we must have protected harbours. On the north side of Prince Edward1 Island we have few harbours, and we do not have the protection we should. In my constituency there is a harbour known as North Rustico, one of the best fishing grounds in the maritime provinces. I do not say it is one of the largest, but there the people really are fishermen, doing nothing else for a livelihood. On several occasions I have appealed to the Minister of Public Works for a wharf or breakwater to protect the houses, shanties and other buildings of the fishermen along that harbour. I am sure that if the matter had been presented to the minister by his engineers in a proper way, he would have seen that the work done so far is absolutely use-

Supply-Fisheries
less. The department should put on an engineer who will take the opinions of 'the fishermen and build something that will not be washed away by the first storm. During the past two years some $10,000 has been spent on 'this protection, but what have we today? We have not had any severe storms, but the work is practically all washed away. A few days ago I recevied a suggestion that the engineers should undertake a survey of that harbour before the fall storms begin; otherwise government property, including the lighthouse, and the buildings of the fishermen will all be washed away.
I have also been advocating the dredging of the bay so that the fishermen can bring their boats up to their own stages. Today they have to leave them a mile and a half away. In 1932 or 1933 this bay was dredged, but since then it has filled up with silt from the land, so that now we have only a narrow channel requiring a fishermen, even at high tide, to anchor his boat away down at the mouth of the harbour and carry his fish ashore. Last year the minister promised that this dredging would be done; but as yet, so far as any benefit to the fishermen goes, it is still only a promise. When we reach the public works estimates I shall forget about fisheries *for a moment and take up that matter with the minister.
As I said, I am going to take up a few other matters as we come to them, and this is all I have to say in a general way. I shall now await the reply of the minister to the two questions I asked, which are found on page 6582 of Hansard.

The May issue of The Bulletin, issued by the fisheries council of 'Canada, has a leading article entitled, "Right Hon. C. D. Howe says fish will be low on priority lists of goods for ERiP," meaning, of course, 'he European recovery plan. The article points out that there is great uncertainty as to what will be the requirements for fisheries products under that plan, and I wonder if the minister could give us some light on that situation. In an address at Winnipeg on May 31 the Minister of Trade and Commerce apparently said 'it was unlikely that there would be much call for fisheries products, and of course that might affect us seriously on the Pacific coast particularly in connection with our canned salmon.

Each country getting support from the Marshall plan decides for itself what products it wants. Our difficulty is to get the various countries to specify fish. In an attempt to have our quota established, we
have been in contact with the Department of Trade and Commerce, and that is about all we can do about the matter. If these countries say they would prefer some other type of food there is nothing we can do about that. We have recognized that this is a possible outlet for some of our fish, and we have done what we could ourselves and have also pressed the matter through the Department of Trade and Commerce.
The decision is made by the country getting the commodities. Is that right?
That is right.
What are the prospects, for example, with respect to the United Kingdom?

I think the hon. member is pretty well acquainted with the situation. Our prospects are not very bright because of the dollar shortage in the United Kingdom. I am afraid that the situation is not as good as we should like to see it.
But I mean under the Marshall plan. Have the British asked for canned salmon or other fisheries products under that plan?

No. The hon. member for Queens asked with respect to the extension of fish inspection. On the east coast we are going just about as quickly as we possibly can with the number of men available. There has been inspection of pickled fish, and recently the department instituted a compulsory inspection of salted fish. The department has already announced its intention to carry out compulsory inspection of canned fish as part of the long-term program to improve quality. On the east coast there are several hundred canneries, however, and as yet the department has not available men with the training necessary to carry on that inspection. Steps are being taken to add to the inspection staff for Prince Edward Island and elsewhere. This new staff, along with the official inspectors and officials of the canned fish laboratories, will work with the cannery operators in giving advice and guidance as to quality control. Meanwhile the Fish Inspection Act is being revised, with a view to giving the department proper authority for compulsory inspection and grading.

The minister referred to these superior types of young men who are entering the outside service of his department in the fish inspection branch. I should like to endorse those sentiments, because a great many of those young men are ex-servicemen.
Supply-Fisheries

However, those who are entering in the lowest grade have 'been discouraged by the wages they are now receiving. Most of them are working for salaries of less than $2,000. Although an increase given earlier this year dated back to October, that increase is not on the same basis as the one which was given to fisheries inspectors grade 2. I would ask the minister to look into this question personally, with respect to salaries paid to the junior officers of his department, namely the grade 1 fisheries inspectors. He will see that the increase made this year for those grade 1 fisheries inspectors was not on the same basis as that made for the grade 2 inspectors. The grade 2 inspectors were given increases based upon their second year of seniority, whereas the grade 1 inspectors received their increases based upon their minimum salary. The young ex-servicemen affected feel that this is not quite fair.
I do not expect the minister to answer this evening, because I realize that in the few minutes now at his disposal he would not be able to look into the situation thoroughly. I am, however, asking him to .make a personal investigation into the matter and to find a way in which he can make the salary increases authorized to grade 1 fisheries inspectors comparable with those authorized for grade 2 inspectors.

I would1 direct the minister's attention to the details as they appear at page 126 of the estimates. According to those details, in 1947-48 there were seventy fisheries inspectors, grade 2; and eight fisheries inspectors, grade 1, or a total of seventy-eight. In 1948-49 there are only seventy altogether, made up of five senior fisheries inspectors, forty-five fisheries inspectors, grade 2, and three fisheries inspectors, grade 1. There is one other group which I do not see at the moment.
I was under the impression that a number of new inspectors were taken into the service and that the service was to be built up. I believed that there were openings for young men, and that a number had applied. I know that in New Brunswick some were taken on. Why is it there are only seventy this year, while there were seventy-eight last year?
This -list gives only the permanent inspectors, and does not show the temporaries. Last year the list included temporary as well as permanent employees.

Why should a different method be adopted this year from that which was used last year? I know these young men in New Brunswick took their examinations and several of them were appointed. I should imagine the same would be true in the other provinces. If

the appointments were made I presume they would be permanent. If the temporary ones are shown in 1947-48, why is there this change in policy in the manner of setting them out?

The temporary employees are not included in this list. It will be recalled that we took on quite a number of young men last year. They are finding their way from the temporary to the permanent list. In the first year they are on a temporary basis, and when they are placed in the permanent service a reallocation is made.
Why are there not more shown this year than there were last? What is the explanation?
This year there are 143 temporaries and 62 permanents.
I understood the minister to say they were all permanent in 1948-49. Apparently that is not correct.
Seventy permanents were employed last year.
Can the minister give a breakdown of the inspectors by provinces?
It would take a little time, but we can get it for the hon. member. I doubt if I could give it tonight.
Are there any permanent guardians? There is an item fishery officers and guardians, and I should like to know if any guardians are employed in addition to inspectors?
All guardians are temporary.

In connection with guardians, could I have a breakdown for the three maritime provinces showing the periods they were employed last year; the periods for this year, if it is no too early to do that; what their duties were; the districts in which they were employed, and what they were paid?
That will require some little calculation, but I shall get it for the hon. member.
I should like to have that.

Item agreed to.
97. Building fishways and clearing rivers, $50,060.

All British Columbia
members have expressed their appreciation at having a British Columbia Minister of Fisheries. I doubt if there is an item in the department's estimates about which we have talked more in the past than this one covering the clearing of streams and the building

Supply-Fisheries
of fishways. I have talked more and got less understanding about this matter, because the previous minister from the maritimes did not understand this British Columbia problem.
Our chief industry in British Columbia is logging, which has a most detrimental effect upon many of our salmon streams. Logging creates stoppages in a great many of these streams, with the result that sockeye and other salmon cannot get up to the headwaters to spawn. We have always protested that this item was hopelessly inadequate; and it may be a welcome sign that it is increased from $25,000 .last year, when the department was under a maritimes minister, to $50,000 this year, when we have a British Columbia Minister of Fisheries. But even that amount is hopelessly inadequate to do the job of clearing many of the smaller salmon streams apart from the Fraser river.
The second matter of building fishways is an old story as far as I am concerned. I have been here eight years and I have seen six different ministers of fisheries. I have in my hand a file which I have built up throughout those years in connection with one little item. The fishermen of Pender Harbour in my riding cannot understand why this bit of work has not been done. Once again I am going to bring forward this little problem at the risk of boring the committee. Perhaps I should not say at the risk of boring the committee, because the hon. member for Queens has quite properly pointed out that this matter of fisheries is of extreme importance to the two maritime coasts of this country. Every session we find that the only opportunity we have to discuss fisheries is on the last night or the second to the last night of the session. Then we are asked, like the hon. member for Timiskaming has just asked me, to hurry up because we want to get through.
We sit here and listen to complaints about wheat and coarse grains, and we never suggest that hon. members talking about those matters should hurry. Therefore I do not feel at all backward about raising problems which are just as important to the fishermen of my riding as are the problems of wheat marketing, coarse grains, fat cows and what have you.
The wheat growers are listening to you now.

That is a courtesy we gave to you, and I ho,pe we can convey our story to hon. members as you have conveyed your story. This is a simple story and it has been often told here. The town of Pender Harbour might be referred to as the Lunenburg of the Pacific coast. It has a landlocked harbour and some excellent fishermen live there who range
the entire coast. Their fishing area is not at home. However, they have a most unusual geographical arrangement, in that there is a small stream three miles from the entrance to the harbour. At one time sockeye salmon were to be found in that stream. It was logged many years ago, and the loggers built a small dam at the entrance to the creek to hold water in Sakinaw lake. When the dam was there the sockeye salmon were able to spawn.
The loggers left and the dam fell into disrepair. Although at that time it would have cost the fisheries department only $900 to repair it, they did not care to do so. When the dam went out, the level of the lake fell, exposing all around the lake for many miles the gravel bars on which the salmon used to spawn. Without the fishway, the salmon were able to get into the lake only at high tide.
Year after year the fishermen of Pender Harbour have asked the department to build a small wooden dam and a small wooden fishway at costs which ranged anywhere from a low of $2,000 to a high of $5,000. There were years when 10,000, 12,000 and 14,000 sockeye salmon were caught at the mouth of that stream. It is a particularly happy fishery, in that it is used by the young boys who are just learning to fish and old men who are too old to go out along the coast of Vancouver island and the Queen Charlotte islands, to the more remote fisheries.
Minister after minister and deputy after deputy, including the present deputy with whom I spoke in private the other evening, as well as the western director, have all said that they would examine into this. They sent a biologist to examine the salinity of the lake. This year, after a visit by the western director to the fishermen's union last fall, they sent an engineer in. They were getting real good. However, they sent in an eastern engineer who knew nothing at all about salmon fisheries, and all he did was to fall into the lake and lose his notes.
When I spoke to the Minister of Fisheries right after he had been appointed about this matter of Sakinaw lake he said he would go there to meet these fishermen. They will be delighted to meet the new Minister of Fisheries, but I do not think they will be over-impressed if once more there is to be another meeting on Sakinaw lake.
I suppose I could ask for an order for return in connection with this matter, but I am quite sure that the total of the travelling expenses for all these officials who have written reports about this matter would more than equal the $5,000 which would be the maximum cost of replacing this dam. I bring this up, so that I can go back to my fishermen at Pender
Supply-Fisheries

Hhrbour and say, "We have a new minister, and once again I have brought up this question in the House of Commons about the public expenditure necessary to restore this real sock-eye salmon fishing". I should like to know from the minister what his plans are for the Sakinaw lake situation and Pender Harbour.

I understand that there are four problems in connection with Sakinaw lake. The first was the salinity, but an inspection has taken place and the conclusion arrived at is that that would n.ot interfere with the fisheries. Another problem is what the spawning beds are like in that area, and an inspection in that connection will be carried out this fall when the fish come up the river. The site for a dam has already been chosen, and it is estimated that it will cost $2,000. The fourth problem is the acquiring of water rights from the provincial government. I can promise the hon. member for Vancouver North that we will give him a definite answer, either yes or no, before the end of the year.

I share the views of the hon. member for Vancouver North. I believe this estimate is very small in comparison with the work there is to be done. I draw the attention of the minister and his parliamentary assistant to conditions on the Red river, where the fish ladders are in very bad shape, and in need of repair. There is not enough water running down the fish ladders for a minnow to climb up, let alone a fish. On the Winnipeg river, one of the largest inland rivers in Canada, which runs from the Lake of the Woods to Lac du Bonnet and empties into lake Winnipeg, where some of the best sturgeon in the country are caught, two big power plants have been established, and there is the immediate prospect of another one being built. The power plants which are there now have no provision for fish ladders, and the consequence is that the fish coming up the river to spawn are stopped and cannot get up. There are no fish above these power plants.

If I may interrupt the hon. gentleman, he is addressing the wrong department. He should go to the fisheries department at Winnipeg. We have no jurisdiction over the area he speaks of. That is a provincial matter entirely.
Was a fishway erected near the mouth of the Nashwaak river near Fredericton, and, if so, what have been the results so far as the salmon are concerned?

Discussions have been going on for a number of years regarding the

dam on this river and its effect on the salmon. It is believed that something may come out of these discussions.

I hope that something will come out of them. I would urge the minister to look into the matter and see if steps cannot be taken, and taken soon, to have a proper fishway put in that dam. There is a beautiful river there.
Experiments have been carried on, but there is no evidence that the dam prevents the fish from going up the river.

What is the position of the fishway at the mouth of the Salmon river beyond St. Martin's in Saint John county? There have been many complaints, which I understand have been looked into with a view to improving conditions.
The officials tell me that plans are in preparation and that the work will be proceeded with this year.

In view of the international treaties in existence, why was no protest made by the Canadian government when the United States built a dam at Grande Coulee on the Columbia river and made no provision for salmon to go up the upper reaches of the Columbia?

That is in the United States, but my understanding is that they did build a fishway at great cost when building the Grande Coulee dam. I do not believe it has been a great success, because the fish in the Columbia river are not going down in numbers.

There is another dam which interferes with the fish getting to their natural spawning grounds. I refer to the dam known as Miller dam at Newcastle Creek, in Queens county, New Brunswick. I have here a letter dated March 15 of this year from Mr. A. J. Hicks, provincial secretary of the New Brunswick fish and game association. He says in this letter:	<
One of the most important issues in respect of fisheries during recent years has been the proposed fishway on the Miller dam at Newcastle creek. The Grand Lake branch has been advocating such a move for the last ten or fifteen years, but without avail. It has been suggested that the dam could very well be dispensed with. Repeated requests have brought assurance from at least two of the recent ministers that such action was contemplated, but that was as far as it went. There is a great deal more to the story, but the last experiment will probably be the installation of the fish trap in order to determine whether or not salmon use the stream for spawning.

Supply-Fisheries
Has that matter been thoroughly investigated, and has any decision been made about either removing the dam or installing a fishway?

At the present
moment the department are carrying on investigations to find out how many fish go up this stream. The investigation has been going on for some years, dating back to 1938, when the question first arose.
Was a trap put in for the first time this year?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
99.	Fish culture, $350,000.

There is a small increase in this vote. The government purchased for the Department of Fisheries a number of old mill dams in the different provinces-I am speaking now of my own constituency-for the purposes of fish culture. Work was started at Simpson's dam and at St. Andrew's dam and was supposed to have been completed two years ago. What progress, if any, has been made with this work? I would also ask what success the department has had with lobster culture on the British Columbia coast?

The hon. member
knows a large number of unused mill dams were constructed at various times in the past for mill operations. The matter he speaks of has received a great deal of consideration over the years, and about two years ago it was decided to carry out investigations to indicate whether, by the reforming of the mill ponds through repairing the dams, the trout industry might be rebuilt. There are problems of reproduction, because a large proportion of the trout runs have been sea-running fish. There is also the matter of the fish population that can be supported in a given area, depending upon the supply of food. Arrangement for the investigation has been made with the province, the fisheries research board and this department co-operating.
I believe the hon. gentleman referred to Simpson's pond. That has been repaired and made ready for operation, and materials are now in process of being obtained for rebuilding a dam at what is known as Andrew's pond near New Glasgow, Prince Edward Island. Another site near Pownal known as Jones' or Worth's pond, has been selected, and it is hoped that the necessary work can be completed early in 1948 or 1949.

Can the minister give an over-all picture of his plans for developing
the industry? This would be an appropriate opportunity for him to do so. Does he intend to do something to increase the fish population throughout the country? If so, by what device? I am not quite sure what the cost of fish culture is throughout the country, and I should like to hear something about the minister's plans.

Perhaps the minister
might also answer the second question asked by the hon. member for Queens as to the success of the work on lobsters on the Pacific coast.

The lobster experiment on the Pacific coast I would not care to describe as a success. Some of the lobsters that were taken out and set free have been lost; but some that were in crates are still living. It is known they have molted, mated and berried as usual, but we cannot say with what conclusion. This is the fifth experiment with lobsters in British Columbia. In Washington they have had a good many and none of them to date have been successful. However, we have not yet had the final report on the last experiment.

Could the minister
give a general over-all picture of his policy with respect to fish culture? I am considerably interested in this, because our fisheries are running down everywhere in Canada and that is not a satisfactory condition. For the last fifty or sixty years the general attitude of Canadians has been that Canada is something to exploit, something out of which we should make all the money we can, leaving the remains to those who come after us. That is poor management, and I cannot think of any way whereby that tendency will be checked except by a determined attitude on the part of the House of Commons. I for one wish to see that trend reversed. I wish to feel that Canada is improving in every respect, building up its forests, farms, fisheries and all the other things that go to make Canada what it is. Is the minister planning a long-range program which would envisage such a process so far as our fisheries are concerned?

I do not wish to take up the time of the committee, but the amount of the estimate is $350,000 for fish culture. What the hon. member wishes to know is our general over-all plan for increasing the fishing industry in Canada. Is that it?

I might be more specific. I have heard the hon. member for New Westminster speak eloquently, enthusiastically and earnestly about the deterioration in
Supply-Fisheries

the salmon industry. I have never heard a minister announce a policy whereby that trend will be arrested and development started in the other direction. I should like to hear a hopeful note. Surely we are not going to allow this industry to deteriorate. The minister speaks of taking up time. Just as the hon. member for Vancouver South has said, every year during the time I have been here it has been my experience that we have never got down to fisheries until the last two or three hours, and then one has almost to apologize for spending some time on the subject. I do not know how we shall develop the fisheries of Canada if we do not take some time in discussing them, to see whether the money we vote for the industry is properly spent. Will the minister give us an assurance that everything is being done to develop the industry.

I must reply to the hon. member. In the first place, the halibut fishery on the west coast had been going down nearly to nil. The halibut commission was formed and it has taken charge of rehabilitation of this fishery. We now have in British Columbia the largest halibut fishing industry-
How long did that take?

It started in 1927. They are doing exactly the same thing with salmon. We have the international Pacific sockeye salmon commission, one of the members of which is the hon. member for New Westminster. We contributed $1,000,000 as Canada's share in building the Hell's Gate fish ladders to increase the run and conserve the fish population of the Eraser river. W'e are spending a considerable sum of money, as will be noted in the estimates, on inspection and research. Our fish last year was worth in the neighbourhood of $120 million to Canada, and we are taking every step to build that up to something near what it should be. I do not know how far we can go, but our difficulty is, in part, to get the fish in good shape into central Canada. We are a little differently situated in Canada from most countries so far as our fish is concerned. Where we have our fish we have a fairly small population, and that is one of the reasons why it is more difficult for Canada to develop fisheries than it is for some other countries.
Can the minister report, in regard to the salmon fisheries, a degree of success comparable with that which he has reported in regard to halibut?

It has not been going on for as long a time. The Hell's Gate ladders

have been in operation for only one year. It is proving a success, and no one denies that it has been a good experiment.
What is the situation on the eastern coast? What is the particular fish about which the people in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are concerned?
On the Atlantic coast, conservation applies to lobsters and oysters, and work is being done in that direction.

What about mackerel and
cod?
They are working on lobsters and oysters just as they have done with salmon.

Are they making
progress comparable with that which the minister has reported in regard to halibut?
They are definitely making progress in lobsters and oysters.

Item agreed to.
100.	Oyster culture, $45,790.

Our oysters on the west coast are mainly from Japanese seed brought in from that country, and of course that was cut off during the war. Has the fisheries research board been able to develop a method with respect to oyster seed for the west coast, so that we can develop this industry in Canada instead of having to rely on Japan?
Experiments are going on now.

With regard to this item for oyster culture, I see there is a small increase this year in the estimate. It should be much larger, because we are not able to develop nearly the amount of oysters that the trade is demanding. What were the royalties collected in 1947, and what were the rental fees for 1947? Is the department considering doing away with royalties on all these leases in 1948?
The royalties on the oysters marketed amounted to $510.45. The lease rentals amounted to $3,030.19. Consideration has not been given to the abolition of the royalties.
The amount collected is so small that it is hardly worth having them.

Item agreed to.
Fisheries Research Board of Canada-
101.	Operation and maintenance, $894,690.

I do not propose to take up very much time of the committee, but I wish to commend any expenditure the Department

Supply-Fisheries
of Fisheries has seen fit to put in under this item 101 this year, or may see fit to put in a like item in any other year for the operation and maintenance of the fisheries research board. My wife happened to christen the ship Harengus, which is used by the joint fisheries board of Newfoundland and Canada for research purposes. That ship has been doing a great deal of good work. I consider our knowledge of fisheries is really only in its infancy. We should do anything that can be done along these lines. We shall learn a great deal in time to come. I shall not take any more time of the committee except to say that I am glad to see that this item has been approved.

This afternoon the hon. member for Nanaimo said something about Canada's giving up her boundaries to the United States. That sounded peculiar to me. If we give up our boundaries to the United States and so on, and if we are getting so close to that country, it seems to me that we should have been represented in Philadelphia in order to have our opportunity to name Dewey as candidate for president of the United States. I am not sure about where we stand.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I should like to offer the minister one suggestion in reference to research work. The United States places scientists on its warships when they are at sea. At points twenty, thirty or forty miles off the coast these fisheries biologists and scientists test the water for salinity, temperature and what is known as plankton, the minute particles in the water which the fish obtain as the water goes through their gills. It is expensive to build or buy or hire a large vessel and crew and send it out to do that kind of work; but the United States have found it convenient and much less expensive to place two or three scientists on their off-shore patrol naval vessels and provide them with the necessary equipment for this experimental and investigational work outside the three-mile limit. So I suggest that this idea might be considered by Canada because I think it is high time we followed along the lines of other nations and found out more about the temperature of the water, the salinity, the plankton and so on, with a view to ascertaining where many of the species of fish go and how they travel.
I hope I have not given the impression that I want to hurry through with these estimates. As a matter of fact, the very opposite is true.
I do not think the minister has given that impression.

I was hoping that I might get a better grasp of the whole industry, and I rather welcome these questions though I do not like to see the committee delayed. I have here a detailed report of what goes on in the various divisions with respect to this research item, and if there is any particular section the hon. member wishes me to deal with I shall be glad to do so. It would take me perhaps twenty-five or thirty minutes to read all the information I have here.

I am not suggesting that. I should like to know, first, whether I am correct in understanding that the department is responsible for the fisheries of the great lakes, as it is for the fisheries of all navigable waters. Am I right in that, to begin with?

No, we do not administer the great lakes. We do administer Great Slave lake and Northwest Territories and the

two coasts. When you look at Canada on a fisheries map it is entirely different from looking at it from an agricultural standpoint. Altogether the coast line is nearly twenty thousand miles long. Therefore a great deal of work has to go on in many different places. This may seem a fairly sizeable amount of money, but when spread over the whole area it really is not so very much. I would offer no apologies for asking that this amount of money be spent on research, a field which is so capable of development and in which so little has been done up to the present time. Rather I would apologize for the smallness of the item.

Still I want to follow this a little. The minister referred to an expenditure of some $20,000 at Toronto. Of course it may be that through some accident you did some work there, even though apparently you are not interested in inland fisheries. If you are not interested and not responsible for the inland fisheries, however, I need not pursue the matter further along that line.

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to a problem which confronts the fresh-water fishing industry in the three prairie provinces. I appreciate that the federal department deals mainly with the salt-water fishing industry, but in the prairie provinces we have a problem known as infestation, which has been serious in recent years. It is quite true that the research branch of the department has done a good deal in endeavouring to find a solution of this problem, but up to the present the situation has not been met successfully. I would urge the minister to look into the matter and see that further scientific work is carried out, in the hope of finding a solution of this problem, since the fresh-water fishing industry in the prairie provinces is important to us, and at the present time it is threatened by this infestation.
The amount to be spent this year in that area for white fish research is $50,000.

In southern central Saskatchewan we do not have much commercial fishing. However, we do have the Winnipeg goldeye, a good, game, valuable little fish, which we can catch in both branches of the Saskatchewan river. There is a mystery in connection with the goldeye, in that it is disappearing and no one seems to know why. I believe the research branch of the fisheries

Supply-Fisheries
department has carried on some investigation, and I am wondering how they are getting along with it and if they are finding any reason for this disappearance. Not so long ago I heard the sergeant-at-arms of this house ask some of the western members where he could get a supply of goldeye for the parliamentary diningroom, which to me is a sign that the supply is limited.
I believe smoked goldeye is almost internationally known to gourmets as a typical Canadian dish. Next to maple syrup it is perhaps the dish known to most people as most typically Canadian. The industry of catching and smoking goldeye is centred in the city of Winnipeg, Manitoba, and the greatest quantities are caught commercially in lake Winnipeg. The goldeye go up the rivers to spawn, and I am interested, owing to the fact that the southern branch of Saskatchewan goes through my home city of Saskatoon.
Various theories have been advanced as to why the goldeye has disappeared. Some people say it is due to disease. Many others hold that it is by reason of the fact that the rivers have been dammed here and there. About 1932 a dam was built across the river near Saskatoon as a relief project; and while fish ladders were built into the dam it is a fact that if you want to find where the fish are you may do so by watching the small boys who go down to the dam to fish on Sunday mornings. You will find that invariably they fish on the side of the dam toward Hudson bay, if I may put it that way. So, if the goldeye are always more plentiful on that side of the dam that seems to be proof that these dams do interfere with the spawning of these fish.
I should like to see something done in this connection. I know the department has been inquiring into the matter. This is something typically Canadian we should try to preserve, and I wish to know if the minister has any information on the matter.

Goldeye investigation
started in 1945, and we hope to have it completed by 1949. Up to date 814,000 has been spent, and the amount appropriated for this year is S4.500. The results of the investigation extended to Alberta, and revealed a new commercial source of goldeye in lake Claire, a western tributary of lake Athabaska. Information has been obtained on spawning, growth, habits, food, physiological tolerance, net mesh size, and effect of dams. The plan is to obtain more detailed spawning information in lake Claire, continue the goldeye studies and develop management practices tc be made effective by regulation. Full information should be obtained on the life history of the goldeye, spawning areas and general distribution, and studies of the causes of depletion of stocks in lake Winnipeg continued. It has been shown that the results from trapping the young fish in the autumn in marshes and shallow lakes of the Saskatchewan delta by a series of dams constructed for the benefit of muskrats, has been one of the main causes of the depletion of this species, and it has been shown that the young fish can be flooded from these areas to deeper water by judicious operation of the dams. These flooding operations have been started, and a marked improvement in supply is anticipated.

I believe that if these fish ladders were made more effective it would have a good effect. There is no doubt that the fish are more plentiful on the north side of the dam than on the south side. One can go there and get a whole bagful of goldeye in a morning on one side of the dam if he knows what bait to use. But on the other side he will get practically nothing. This appears to prove conclusively that these fish dams are not sufficiently easy to get up, if I may put it that way.
How is this appropriation being spent? The minister has told us that some research is going on. What about the actual spending of the money?

The money is being spent for payment of the scientists who are doing that work at the present time. We have scientists who are studying the goldeye. We hope they will be able to make a full report in 1949.

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
That question was raised earlier in the session and I made a reply based on a statement made earlier by the Minister of Finance in connection with civil service superannuation, that these pensions were matters of contract and these pensioners were in exactly the same category as others with regard to pensions. Supply-National Defence
altered without changing everything that had happened up to then. It would be difficult to change a particular category. The hon. member who raised the question will appreciate that those who are enjoying pensions on account of their service in the armed forces, and those who may enjoy pensions in the armed forces are in a favourable position compared with either civil servants or other employees in Canada. We feel that ithe matter is one which must be regarded in its entirety and that it would be impossible to differentiate between one class and the other. But I would point out something which I think the hon. member knows very well, and that is that pensioners who are former members of the armed forces are in a favourable position compared with the others.

I realize the difficulties that exist in this particular respect, but I cannot agree with the minister that the pensioners under the Militia Pension Act are in more favourable circumstances than personnel who are drawing pensions from other government pension schemes such as the civil service. I would point out that these men have been on service during a large portion of their lives; and, while it may not be possible to increase the pension, I suggest to the minister, in view of the fact that recently the Department of Veterans Affairs have opened hospitals across the country to personnel who are in receipt of war veterans allowance, he should confer with the Minister of Veterans Affairs to see whether it is not possible to enable those old soldiers, sailors and airmen now pensionable to have the advantages of veteran hospitals on the same basis as those recipients of war veterans allowance. Supply-National Defence

that he took some credit for the fact that the army had recruited up to 76 per cent of that total.
This is the first time I have heard of this target figure, and I must say it is a unique method of bringing units up to strength by cutting the establishment in half and then declaring that the unit is approximately 70 per cent of strength. A somewhat similar case, and I fancy a more serious one too, is that in connection with the Royal Canadian Air Force auxiliary squadrons. In 1946 the figure was set at 4,500. Yes. The first question raised by the hon. member was with regard to the figure set for the establishment of the reserve army, at a total which he gave as 187,864, which I have not had a chance to verify but which I accept. That is the establishment set out by my predecessor for a reserve army of six divisions, which would be the scale of organization for all Canada in the event of an emergency. But I think the hon. member would be the first to admit, on the basis of his own experience, that anything like that figure would be quite out of the possibility of our raising in peacetime. Establishments are set by units and by strengths, and they are intended to be a description of the force that we would have in the event of a total mobilization. When that was set out, I think the minister of defence of the time indicated that the target for that particular year was something a great deal less; and from year to year the defence services set their targets based on what they believe they can train and on what they believe they can get. Both factors are taken into consideration.
The figures for the navy, army and air force for this year were set out by me in my statement yesterday at page 5782 of Hansard. There is no need to repeat them. But the figure set out for an establishment of six divisions remains as it was set out by my predecessor, in 1945, at the figure described by the hon. member. There is a difference

between the establishment and what one can do with activated units and their staffs of officers, N.C.O.'s and men.

Yes, I agree. I think the minister will recall that I referred some years ago to the fact that this original figure was a foolish and boastful statement to make. I am quite certain that it is beyond the realm Of possibility. I want to emphasize the fact that here we started out with an organization, as the minister has just said, based on six divisions. He found1 in 1947 that it was impractical to get anywhere near that number, so he reduced it until we were down to 90,000. Then, because he has found this year that it is impractical to reach that figure, he has cut it in half again. The semblance of six divisions has gone up in air; it has vanished. There is not even the vaguest skeleton. You may have it on paper, but when you have cut so drastically as that, I think you will agree with me that the idea of six divisions is at the moment not within the realm of reality.
I wish to emphasize this point. It is just supporting what I said yesterday that we are trying to build on time-honoured, though time-worn-out formations, and present conditions require an entirely different approach to this subject of national defence. I think this is strong evidence in support of what I said then.
May I ask another question with regard to the strength of the active army, particularly the field force? We have been told the units-or if we have not been told, I think it is generally known-comprising the field force or, as it has sometimes been referred to, the mobile brigade. But he may feel that, for the purposes of security, it is not advisable to give that information. If he will give the total, well and good. But if he can give us the numbers by units, I should like to have that information.

With regard to the hon. member's first remarks, there is a great deal in what he said with which I might agree. But the idea of setting out a six divisional set-up is not to provide targets from year to year for us to aim at, but rather to provide the nucleus upon which we could build and organize should a national emergency occur. There was never any intention, as he knows, that we should recruit to anything like the strength of 187,000.
With regard to the mobile group, as he himself suggests there may be some reasons

of security why we should not give the actual strength, unit by unit. I can tell him that, of the present total strength of men in the army of Canada, about twenty per cent are in the mobile brigade. Our expectation is that that percentage will increase as recruiting goes on. As I indicated yesterday, the armoured and infantry battalions are undergoing unit training at Petawawa and also at Wainwright, Shilo, Chilliwack and Valcartier; and this will be the first summer in which we will be able to have unit training for that force. As I think the hon. member knows-and I will be frank with him-it will be extremely difficult for us to protect that force from other demands. When, for example, the emergency occurred in the Fraser valley, the training of some units had to be interfered with, when they were sent from as far away as Calgary; and every now and then a demand for an extra commitment is made from here or there. On that account I was very glad indeed to be able to announce yesterday that we are going to recruit over and above our target, so that we hope to build up the force as speedily as possible, and train it as well as that may be done.
Then I take it that this is the first year in which any grouping of these regiments into a field brigade has taken place?

As battalions, that is
right.
This the first time as units?
That is right.

So, that, as a mixed
brigade or brigade group they have not yet had any training as such?
That is right.

Then the minister referred to the Fraser valley, where a number of reserve army units have been training. Will the personnel of those units be authorized to carry out their annual thirty days training in addition to the time they have spent in the flooded area?

Yes, they certainly are authorized, and the army would be very glad to see them do it. But these men have already given from their ordinary civilian occupations periods of time dating from May 23, when the first unit came out on active service in Kimberley. Whether or not they will be able to devote more time to training this year will depend on the individual unit, but we shall be prepared to provide pay and allowances for every officer and man, who may be qualified to
train, in addition to anything they may have received in respect of the service they rendered in the flooded area.
Even though that training is done at local headquarters and not in camp?
Yes.
Because all these units give additional time?
Right.

I am not going to take up much more time, but I want to ask one question regarding the Royal Canadian Air Cadet Corps. In the past it has been customary to take these lads to some camp adjacent to or right in one of the R.C.A.F. stations and give them certain instruction in regard to the machines generally. In addition, some of the boys are permitted to have flights, in order that they may become air-minded in the early stages. But before they are permitted to go up as passengers, they have to obtain waivers from their parents. That is acting as a deterrent to some of these boys because their parents are not prepared to sign the waiver. They feel that, as long as the boys are in the uniform of the R.C.A.F. and training, perhaps with the idea of ultimately joining the auxiliary service, they should not be required to do so. Surely we have sufficient confidence in the R.C.A.F. to believe that there is the minimum of risk involved when these boys are taken up. If we want to encourage them to take an interest in the air arm, surely this country can afford to accept whatever risk there may be. So I would ask the minister if for the future he will cancel the regulation which makes it necessary for an R.C.A.F. cadet in uniform to obtain from his parents a waiver in favour of the government before he is permitted to go up on a sight-seeing or passenger flight.

Royal Canadian Air Force cadets may fly either with R.C.A.F. pilots in R.C.A.F. planes or, as is the case with the great majority, in planes of the royal flying clubs, which are civilian-owned and operated, and work under contract with the Department of National Defence. I am not quite sure whether waivers were required in the first instance; I would rather doubt it. They might have been required in the second case, but certainly I shall look into the whole question. As a matter of fact, this business of waivers with regard to liability in respect of people flying in R.C.A.F. planes has been the subject of active consideration by the department over the last five or six months. It involves difficult legal problems; and the bill I had hoped to introduce in the house to deal with all these
Supply-National Defence

matters had a clause with respect to it. We are still looking into the matter, and I shall be glad to take the hon. member's representations into consideration.
I know that last year cadets flying in R.C.A.F. planes were required to obtain waivers before they went up.

I want to make a short reference to the sea cadet movement. As I pointed out to the then minister of national defence tiwo years ago, when pay and allowances were brought in for the officers on the training establishment for sea cadets, any remuneration they received should be in the form of allowances, because their pay is subject to tax. That creates a hardship on these men who are training the sea cadets. I have personal knowledge of these matters, because for several years during the war I was active in the sea cadet movement. Hardly a month goes by when these sea cadet officers do not provide out of their own funds something for the boys in their units. That always has been and probably always will be the case, and it is a hardship to put them on pay and then have that pay taxed in some cases up to a considerable percentage of the total. That is not encouraging. I bring this matter to the minister's attention because I consider it to be unfair.
I should like to ask one or two questions with respect to the navy. I am sure the minister is quite conversant with the situation, but I would remind him that a year ago one of the great complaints in Halifax was that the married personnel did not have suitable housing accommodation for their families. I know several chaps who were extremely interested in their work, but who were greatly dissatisfied because their families could not be properly housed in Halifax and, in some cases, had to remain in central Canada. Perhaps the minister would state just what the situation is now.

With respect to the men who, as the hon. member quite rightly said, and as I agree, give their time to the work of the sea cadets and then find their pay subject to income tax, I would point out that they are in the same category as all members of the reserves of the three services. That involves a large question which I am afraid I must leave on the lap of my hon. colleague the Minister of National Revenue. I have had some discussions with the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance in this connection, because I feel, with the hon. member for Wentworth, that it is an important consideration. Having been,

as I think he was, one who served and gave all his pay for some considerable time to this kind of work, it is hard to pay income tax on it after you have given it away. So I can assure the hon. member I have made representations to my colleague ,and I shall be reinforced in those representations by the remarks he has just made.
I must say, of course, that from their point of view there is the desirability of trying to get everyone in Canada to pay income tax. Those are two factors to be considered. We would like very much to have this pay and allowances for part-time servants of Canada in the reserve forces when they are working in the navy, the army, the air force or the cadets regarded in the same category. But thus far we have not been able to work it out. I shall keep the matter in mind however, and I shall be glad to put forward the hon. member's representation.
With regard to married personnel at Halifax, we have, as he knows, a program for building married quarters which I announced in the house a month ago. The number of units planned for Dartmouth is eighty in the next year, and that will do quite a lot toward relieving the worst of the situation there.
Have any been completed in the last year?
Quite a number of conversions have.
That is additional accommodation.
Yes.

Another matter I would bring to the minister's attention is a complaint made by many of the naval personnel stationed at, we will say, Halifax, whose homes are in central Canada. They find it difficult to pay their fares on their annual leaves. Has any consideration been given to issuing an annual warrant for annual leave to their home destinations?

That is a matter under active consideration. If it were only a question of the navy which, as the hon. member knows, is centred chiefly on the two coasts, at Halifax and Esquimalt, it would not be a very difficult-matter. But we have tried to put all three services on an exactly equivalent basis with regard to pay and allowances. Once you step out of that extreme situation of Halifax or Esquimalt, you get into the realm of considering such places as Borden, Shilo, Rivers, Chilliwack, Valcartier and so on, with all the difficulties involved in trying to arrive at some basis of a fair allowance. That is a matter under active consideration.
