I know some months ago there were some complaints about food in the navy, especially when personnel -were at sea. Has the allowance for food per day per man been raised in the past twelve months? I believe it was sixty-tiwo cents per man per day a year ago. Is that correct? Has the allowance been advanced since then?

The ration has not been increased, but the cost of the ration has increased in accordance with the increase in the cost of living. I might say that, to provide for conditions at sea, the navy receives an extra allowance over and above that received by the army and air force personnel. I believe the amount is five cents a day. I must say my experience, from moving around and eating meals served the men in a great many establishments and ships is that, by and large, the meals are very good. I might not have arrived at the right time, but I have sat down with literally hundreds of men and talked with them and never had complaints about the food. I have had lots of complaints-but never about the food. If there is any complaint about it I would suggest that it is not due either to the amount provided to buy food or to the size of the ration. It might be due to the conditions of service, or the way in which the food is presented. We are trying to improve that steadily in the navy, as in the other two services.
The hon. member, who is very much interested in this, might find some considerable improvement in that respect within the last twelve months.

I have had some little experience. There is one thing I do know about the navy, and that is that, generally speaking, the officers get the same food as the men. Probably, when the minister was dining he was in the wardroom.
There is another matter I should like to bring to his attention, and this applies to the men at sea. It is not right that they should eat their meals in quarters where their clothing is hanging and where different equipment is scattered about. If a cafeteria system were set up, and it were placed in a location apart from their sleeping quarters, it would be a great improvement.
In this respect I believe the United States navy allows, or some months ago did allow, $1.10 a day per man for food alone. I understand that food in the United States navy is very good. I believe the complaint in the Royal Canadian Navy has not been as to the quality of the food. While it may have the required calories, it does not have the bulk. I believe that if many of these young lads had 5849-374J
more bulk it would solve much of the difficulty. If they received more bulk they would be better satisfied. They complain about the small quantity of food. The nutrition may be there, the calories and all that sort of thing which they require for sustenance, but they do not think they receive enough of it. That is something the department should consider.

I can assure the hon. member that I am very much interested in this question of food for the troops. One of my sins for a very short period of time was that I was a quartermaster sergeant in world war I. It is a confession I have never made before.
I always thought you were a sergeant major.

I graduated from the first post to the second. On that account, as well as others, I have been interested in this subject; and when I have made inspection tours I have found, as have other hon. members who have had the experience of inspecting, that things tend to be a little laid on. I have two or three things that are of particular interest; one is fire protection and prevention; another is food, and another is living accommodation.
Were you ever a cook?

No.
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Wentworth, I did have the good fortune to visit San Francisco last August on my way to Australia. While there, I did a most improper thing. I was being shown over a dockyard by the admiral who was in charge of arranging the tour, and suddenly I said to him, "Do you mind if I see the messing accommodation in one of your destroyers? I have heard that they are better than ours in that respect". He said, "No, not at all; step aboard anyone you see". We went aboard a destroyer in process of refitting, and went over it. It was rather like our Tribal class in size and style. I saw there the messing and bunking accommodation, and also their cooking arrangements. I had just been over one of our Tribal class; in fact I spent a day on her, so I had become familiar with the accommodation. I must say that, in consequence of that, I am not sure which system is the better. If you divide the accommodation available for the men into bunking arrangements and messing accommodation you have very much constricted quarters. I am not too sure that our arrangement is not the better.
With regard to the galley and refrigeration arrangements and all that, ours were just as good as theirs. It was an interesting experience; and it left me, being interested in the
Supply-National Defence

subject, with an open mind. Certainly it is a thing that has to be followed up and watched.
With regard to the cafeteria system, we follow that almost entirely throughout the shore establishments and big ships. It is applied in part on the small ships.
I notice that the amount for the sea cadets is increased this year. Is that because of increased camp accommodation, or has the service grown?
The arrangements with regard to the sea cadets provide for the same number, but the cost of accommodation has increased.

In order to preserve a
quorum in the chamber, may I suggest that the radio, which is being listened to with such rapt attention out in the lobby be moved either into the chamber or into the opposition or government lobby, so that we can all hear it. It seems to me that bon. members are more interested in the Louis-Walcott fight than in transacting business. May I make another suggestion? While the minister is giving full and complete replies to the questions being asked, it seems to me that his replies might be more brief and not take up so much time. We are not going to finish much business tonight.

There are four or five questions I should like to ask, the first having to do with the reserve army. In other days it was recognized that if Canadian troops had to fight they would be fighting abroad, and that gave a longer time in which to train our forces. Now we hear that any war which may occur may be fought, at least partly, in Canada. When the minister and his predecessors have spoken of the armed forces they have always emphasized that fact.
As we all know, we are to have a small active army. There is to be only one mobile force, which at the moment is not recruited up to strength. The main force is to consist of the reserve army. It was pointed out back in 1945 that the policy was to have six divisions and, I think, two corps staffs. I have the Hansard here, and the minister's predecessor stated at that time that the total number would be between 135,000 and 150,000. It is now evident that we are not going as far as he had planned in making preparations for the building up of that force.
How long does the department consider it will take to put that reserve army into the field as a fighting force? I think we are entitled to have that information. It may very well be that the plans are such that the

force could not be put into the field for a long time. If the job is to defend Canada in these days of warfare in the air, in these days of no warning that war is coming, the reserve force may never have a chance to get into action. That is one of the key factors to keep in mind when we are determining what our defence measures should be. Can the minister answer that question?

That is one of those questions where one would have to know when the war broke out, who the prospective enemy was and what he was doing. I cannot answer that question. If it is related to invasion of Canada, then by whom-I should like to ask that-and with what force?
I do not think that is a fair question for the minister to put to me. He said yesterday that a certain nation could send over 1,000 planes.
I never said anything of the kind; I said exactly the opposite.
That they might send them over.
I did not say that.

Then let us forget about that. I think the minister went pretty far yesterday in the statement he did make. But surely the department has in mind how long it would take to put the reserve army into the field. Suppose war were to break out a month from now or in six months from now; how long would it be before we had that reserve army in the field? I point out to the minister that this is vital, because that is the force on which we must depend for our defences. If the department cannot give that information then I think it should be able to.

Neither this department nor any other department in any country of the world can give that unless you give the assumptions on which we have to work. You give Us those, and I will give you or I will get my experts to give you the answers. I am not going to give any carte blanche answer to that kind of question, because there is no doubt that I would be wrong.

I do not ask for the exact length of time, but surely the department must know approximately how long it would take to field the reserve army.
Mr. CLAXTON; For what purpose, where and when?

In Canada, for the defence of Canada.

Supply-National Defence
We can do a certain job tomorrow and a much bigger job next week and so on. It will go on, on that basis.
Of course that is really no answer at all. I take it from the answer the minister has given that he does not know.

I know how difficult it is to answer that kind of question unless I have the facts and assumptions on which it can be answered. I have seen enough of staff course problems that are put to staff officers to know they must have the assumptions on which to give answers. You give me the assumptions and I will get the staff officers to give you the answers, but I cannot give answers without the assumptions.
I suggest that the minister put his staff to work on that question.
They have worked on questions of that kind. If you provide the assumptions they will provide the answers.

When the minister is expecting the citizens of Canada to form an army on a voluntary basis, some guidance should be given to them, more than is being given by these answers this evening. We have to get down to bedrock to a much greater degree than the minister has done.
Just about a month ago there appeared a Canadian Press dispatch in the Vancouver papers, headed and reading as follows:
U.S. still maintains two bases in north. Canadian landing fields kept up by Americans to prevent disuse, Ottawa, May 25.
Defence department officials have confirmed a Washington report that members of the United States armed forces still are maintaining two Canadian landing bases on Canada's northeastern frontier.
The Washington report said housing facilities were being built by the United States at Frobisher Bay and Fort Chimo.
It was understood the maintenance crew was a carry-over from the second world war, when the then highly-secret "Crimson Route" was established. The route was a series of landing fields established for short-range aircraft being ferried across the Atlantic.
Since the war, rather than have the air fields fall into disuse, Canada had agreed with the United States that the fields be maintained by American personnel, an official said.
Why should Canada not be manning these two posts herself? Why do we have to have the United States manning these two posts in northeastern Canada?

In consequence of our arrangements for joint defence, the United States undertakes certain jobs and the Canadian government undertakes certain jobs. The United States asked our agreement to
their rebuilding some of the quarters at Chimo and Frobisher Bay which were unfortunately falling into a state of disrepair, and also to building some married quarters. Those married quarters are being built for us at our expense as well as for them. We agreed to that being done. At the same time we are doing joint operations for them in our north. At one place it is convenient for one country to do it, and at another it is convenient for the other country to do it.
Is there any reason why Canada should not be manning her posts herself? It would be perfectly all right to let the United States use them, but why should Canada not man them herself?
Why should the Americans not contribute to the cost of manning posts which they themselves are occupying in accordance with our arrangements? I cannot see any objection to that.
It is all right for them to contribute, but why should Canada not be manning these posts rather than the United States?

I am not too sure about those two posts. There are three posts, I think, in Canada, and they are rather small ones, in respect of which the number of United States personnel is larger than the Canadian personnel. That is only three out of quite a number. Generally speaking, there is a Canadian in charge and there are more Canadians than Americans in these places. If there are any exceptions it is because the United States has a particular interest in a particular place, but gradually we will take care of that.

I suggest to the minister that these two posts should be manned by Canadians. Let the Americans use them all they wish, but I cannot see any reason why we should not be manning them with our own personnel.
Another question has to do with the Canadians who served at Hong Kong. As the minister knows, these men have not yet been given Pacific pay. The 1,600 odd men who were recruited in 1945 to go to the Pacific did receive Pacific pay; but these other young men who went to Hong Kong in 1941 and suffered hardships and abuse such as no other Canadian troops have ever suffered since confederation, are not paid Pacific pay. The matter has been raised in the house on other occasions, and just this week we find in the report of the special committee on veterans affairs that a brief was heard by the committee which was submitted by the veterans of Hong Kong. The
Supply-National Defence

committee forwarded the brief to the Department of National Defence because, of course, the committee had no power to act upon it, since they were dealing only with questions having to do with the Department of Veterans Affairs.
We on the Pacific coast feel deeply about this matter. These young men went out from Vancouver harbour on that ill-fated expedition. Many of them are now in hospital in Vancouver, and we can tell by looking at the men themselves, even though they are fit, wdiat they have been through. On June 21 an editorial appeared in the Vancouver Province, entitled, "Must They Fight Twice for their Pay?" I think that editorial sums up the sentiment of Canadians from coast to coast with regard to these Hong Kong veterans. I do not think any reason can be given for withholding from them that Pacific pay. Certainly paying them the difference between the old rate of pay and the Pacific rate of pay can be no compensation to them for the sufferings they endured in Japanese prison camps, and I hope that the minister can announce to the committee tonight that these men are to receive the Pacific pay. May I have an answer?
If pay were any compensation for sufferings-
It wrnuld be some.

-I would be only too happy to make the announcement my hon. friend wants. This question has been before the government since, I think, late in 1945. It has been considered on a considerable number of occasions. I have had quite a number of communications from the Hong Kong Veterans Association of Canada, and the matter has been given active consideration. Since then, that association has appeared and made a very good presentation to the committee on veterans affairs. I shall be very glad that the matter be once more brought before the cabinet for consideration.

My final question has to do with the financial assistance given to the reserve units. I have received a submission from a commander of one of the units on the * Pacific coast. As the minister knows, I have shown him that communication. This commanding officer suggests that there should be an allowance to each regiment cf between $3,000 and $4,000 a year. His particular regiment is now getting $824.18 a year. He is an officer with an excellent fighting record overseas and an excellent record in the non-penmanent active militia before the war. He has gone back to the command of his regi-
ment and was out on duty with it for several weeks during the floods in British Columbia. I think his submission is absolutely correct. He points out, if I may quote two paragraphs from his letter:
To the writer's knowledge, based upon some years of experience in the non-permanent active militia and the reserve -army, N.P.A.M. units and reserve army units by and large have never received sufficient military allowances from the government to cover the actual cost of running the units, the operating deficits of these units being made up -by donations of pay from serving personnel-
Not only from the officers but also from the men.
-or by donations from wealthy benefactors, or both.
It is the writer's strong conviction that reserve army units should receive government allowances in accordance with the type, strength and location of the unit, sufficient in amount to enable the commanding officers to run a successful and aggressive unit without having to depend upon donations from either within or without the unit to cover such expenses.
Our reserve army is serious business. We are expecting it to defend this country, and I think the day has gone by when the officers and men should be compelled to put up their own money or go and find a sugar daddy and make him an honorary lieutenant-colonel or an honorary colonel in order to get the finances with which to run the regiment. I do not think that is in line with the beliefs of the Canadian people. I do hope that at the present time some better arrangement can be made for the financing of these reserve units.

This question has been an active one with the department for-a number of years, and last year we had a meeting with the council of defence associations, representing the various corps of the Canadian army. The consequence of that was to increase the unit allowances and change the capitation grants in respect of each unit. Since then, we have had two meetings of members of the council representing the reserve associations, and they are giving us figures on how this is working out.
I think ou-r feeling is along the lines of those represented by the hon. member for Vancouver South, and that some further adjustment must be made. We are in close touch with the representative of the reserve associations and the matter is receiving active consideration. Our expectation is that some further grant may be made.

I wish to support as strongly as I can the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South in regard to the Hong Kong veterans, and it will not take me more than a few sentences to state my position. I was pleased to hear the minister say that his

Supply-National Defence
department was still considering it sympathetically, but I must add that eighteen months constitute quite a long time to have had the matter under consideration, and action is about due. In fact, it is long overdue.
These men are being denied their just rights on the merest of technicalities. There is no need for me to argue their case tonight, their cruel imprisonment and their great courage.
I wish the minister had been present when they presented their brief in the veterans affairs committee.
I had already received it.

I am glad to hear that. They showed great sportsmanship. They did not come with a grievance but came simply to give us the facts. The Canadian people were,
I know, glad to do everything they could to rehabilitate Canada's veterans. That was one thing that went through the house with unanimous consent, if we ever had unanimous consent. The Canadian people do not want this matter left on their doorstep. If they owe a debt to any of the veterans of Canada for their service during the last war they owe it to the Hong Kong veterans, and they do not want it left on their doorstep. I hope the minister will be able to get his department to come to a decision shortly.

As I have listened to the debate, and I have done so for quite a while, I confess that a feeling of bewilderment has come over me. I did not know whether I was taking part in a solemn farce. Either we believe that we need some defence, or we do not. One hon. member last night assured us that we did not need any, because he could give us his assurance that no danger would arise. Unfortunately, I cannot say the same. As I say, I have had a feeling of bewilderment; I did not know whether this was a serious discussion or a sort of Gilbert and Sullivan comedy.
Apparently we have a skeleton; not a complete skeleton, I gather. As I listened to the hon. member for Nanaimo describing what was going on, that feeling of bewilderment which I have already suggested came upon me all the more forcibly, coupled with a sense of a farcial element in this whole matter. Take the "target". That struck me as a most diverting idea. You have an establishment which you cannot reach, so you cut it in two, and when you cannot reach it you cut it in two again. It reminds me of the story of the man who came to a banker with a number of worthless stocks on which he wished to borrow money. He valued them high enough to show a surplus, and the banker said, "Mr. Smith, if vou only valued all those securities at twice
as much, you would have twice as great a surplus." I think we are in very much the same position.
When I heard the minister say, not without some complacency, as I thought, that we were almost as good as we were in 1939 or thereabouts, it struck me that there were farcical elements in that too, because we all remember the position in which we found ourselves in 1939.
I do not wish to stop there and leave the impression that I am blaming the minister or that I think the minister has no answer. In one way, he has a perfect answer, and I think he has given this perfect answer. That answer is that he cannot get people to enlist, that we know there is full employment, and that we know, therefore, that conditions are such that we can have only a skeleton of a skeleton.
But my complaint is this. The people of Canada are not allowed to know that. If the people of Canada knew they had only a skeleton force, a force that could not do anything; if they knew they were defenceless, and if, having that knowledge, they said, "All right", that would be up to them. If they have no patriotism left, or if they accept the view of the hon. member for Cape Breton South, that there is no danger facing them, that is their concern. But I suggest that it is the duty of the government to tell us the truth, to let the people of Canada know the truth, and not to let items appear in the press such as I read yesterday. I read an item in the press yesterday to the effect that the Minister of National Defence was quoted as saying we could defend ourselves against 1,000 aeroplanes. I thought he must have been misunderstood. But there, again, I do not blame the minister.
You do not blame me for what appears in the press, do you?

No, but I am blaming the minister for this, that the impression has been left throughout the whole course of this debate that things are not so bad; that we are doing not so badly; that there is nothing really much to worry about, and so on. My complaint is that the people are not being told the truth. The people should be told the truth; we here should be told the truth, and if the people are told the truth and they accept the situa-ion, that is up to them.

I can hardly allow the minister's answer to the hon. member for Vancouver South to pass without some challenge, and that is regarding the length of time it would take to put some of our forces
Supply-National Defence

in the field. It is inevitable that, in the proposals to which the minister referred yesterday, plans must be drawn up as to when the first division, or the second or the third division, could be mobilized if they were required. Similar plans existed, to my knowledge, in 1939. We had the example of 1939. We know how long it took for the first division to leave these shores. War broke out in the early part of September, and in early December the first division, untrained, left Canada to complete its training in the United Kingdom, where fortunately it had quite an extended period before being required to go into action.
I am not going to press the minister to give an answer. I do not believe it is in the interests of the security of the country that he should give an answer, but I refuse to accept the idea that no plans are made as to when, under certain sets of circumstances, troops can be made readily available. I suggest that it is not in the interests of security to announce those plans, but I wish that we might have a little more honesty in that respect. I have mentioned the time it took for the reserve army as trained in 1939 to be able to leave Canada to go to the war in that year. I do not think there is any need to labour the point.
I said yesterday that the reserve army is no more efficient today than it was in 1939. It has not had unit training. The minister admitted, and it is known everywhere, that we have been concentrating on the training of officers and non-commissioned officers. I do not know that anyone will grumble with that policy, but the fact remains that it is highly doubtful whether the first division of the reserve army today could be mobilized any more speedily than was the case in 1939.

I wish to follow up the point made^ by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and refer to the situation in connection with enlistment in Canada. I say to the minister it is my sincere belief, though there may have been improvement lately, that his difficulties with proper recruiting stem from one source and one source only, and that is the rates of pay which the armed services are offering. I think he told us in his speech that they had increased by ten per cent. As the minister well knows, the cost of living has gone away beyond that. It has risen 50 per cent. The cost of food is 90 per cent above what it was in 1939.
These rates of pay are quite out of line with present-day living costs. More than that, they are technically out of line, because the soldier, the sailor and the airman of today are quite different fighting men from what they were in 
1914-18 or perhaps even in 1939. As the minister said in his speech, the infantry man has at least six different sets of weapons to learn; the sailor must be a specialist in wireless, radar or some other technical side of naval work; and, as we all know, the airman has a tremendous number of technical requirements to fulfil before he is of any use in that sphere.
These men have jobs they can do in industry. If the minister wants them to go into Canada's active service forces, he must offer them a rate of pay that is at least somewhat competitive, and a ten per cent increase over the rates of pay during the war is certainly not enough to attract men with the technical capacity to master the techniques required in the armed forces of 1948.

It makes me feel ashamed to be a Canadian when I learn that the Hong Kong men are still being considered instead of their being rewarded for the kind of experience they went through. Then they went through probably the most awful experiences that any group of men in the war went through. In many cases their health was permanently destroyed. Their chances for happiness are, in most cases, gone, if I am correctly informed. Now we hear albout their being considered, instead of being rewarded as heroes of that kind ought to be rewarded.
I would say in a general way that if the minister wants an explanation of why his recruiting is not progressing as he would like it to progress, he will find one of 'those reasons in the fact that rumours have gone over this land concerning the way in which we have treated the Hong Kong men. I wonder how many would vote to see their boys go in there? I will wager that not a single one in this house would do so. That being so, how can one expect other people to want their boys to go into the army when there is

The college is being reconstituted., as I understand it, and I should like to ask the minister whether it is the aim of the college to follow its former practice? I cannot see the difficulty in the remarks of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. The idea back of the institution of the Royal Military College at Kingston is that we shall have for the three services a training institution which will provide the youth of Canada with a training second to none, measured by university standards, during the academic year; then, in the summer months, it will lead to their spending three and a half months on practical work with the service they select in the branch of the armed services for which they are fitted. Our expectation is that we shall establish new standards in this college equivalent to those of the universities throughout Canada, and that the men who graduate from our college will be well qualified to serve their country either on a full-time basis as members of the active forces or on a parttime basis as members of the reserve forces, but, above all, as citizens of Canada.

I am afraid I did not make my question plain to the minister. I will state it a little bit differently. What I want to know is whether the military college, in addition to doing those things that I assume it would do-and they are obvious enough-would attempt, as far as possible, to take the place of what we might call post-graduate work and research work in the ordinary civilian university.

No, not at all. It is not a post-graduate college. It is a college which will train the men who go through it in work which is equivalent to under-graduate work in the universities. It is equivalent for the first two years, year by year; and then, if carried on to the full four-year course, it will be equivalent to three years of engineering in the university. Post-graduate work in the armed forces will be carried on with the army staff college, the air staff college and the national defence college.
